title: Glossary
text:
1 · What you hear → · Glossary
Each entry gives a plain definition and a link to a fuller explanation.

title: Glossary
text:
Sound

Sound

The air pressure p(t) at a listener, measured from the average air pressure; it travels as a wave, at about 343 m/s at 20 °C. Wikipedia

Hertz (Hz)

One cycle per second, the unit of frequency. The A above middle C is tuned to 440 Hz. Wikipedia

Pure tone

The simplest sound, a single sinusoidal pressure swing c\sin(2\pi f t + \varphi) with frequency f, size c and phase \varphi, which says where in its cycle it starts. A tuning fork’s sound is close to one. Wikipedia

Partial, overtone

A partial is one sinusoidal component c_n\sin(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n) of a sound, with its own frequency f_n, size c_n and fading. An overtone is any partial above the lowest. Wikipedia

Harmonic

A partial at a whole-number multiple nf of a base frequency f: the n-th harmonic. A harmonic sound is one whose partials are all harmonics of one base, so its first overtone is the second harmonic. Wikipedia

Harmonic series

The whole-number multiples f, 2f, 3f, \dots of one frequency f. Wikipedia

Periodic

A signal p(t) is periodic with period P > 0 if p(t + P) = p(t) for all t. A sum of steady partials is periodic exactly when all their frequencies are whole-number multiples of one frequency (post 1). Wikipedia

Repetition rate

This series’ term: for steady partials at exact whole-number multiples of a common frequency, 1 over the shortest period, which is the largest such frequency, so partials at 440, 660 and 880 Hz repeat at 220 Hz. For partials that fade or sit only near multiples, it is the largest frequency in the range we hear as pitch that they fit within a stated tolerance (post 1). Wikipedia: Fundamental frequency

Fundamental

For a harmonic sound, the partial at its repetition rate: usually the lowest and strongest, but it can be weak or missing and the pitch is still heard there. For a sound whose partials are not harmonics of one base, such as a drum’s, it just means the lowest partial. Wikipedia

Pitch

A perception: how high or low a sound is, measured as the frequency of the pure tone listeners match it to. When the partials f_n are whole-number multiples of one frequency f_1, the pitch is f_1, even if that partial is weak or missing; post 1 gives the exceptions. Wikipedia

Missing fundamental

A harmonic sound with no partial at its repetition rate, such as partials at 440, 660, 880, … Hz with nothing at 220 Hz; the ear still hears its pitch at 220 Hz. It is why a deep voice keeps its pitch over a telephone line that carries little below about 300 Hz. Wikipedia, and post 1

Sound pressure level, decibel 

The decibel (dB) measures a ratio on a logarithmic scale: two powers in the ratio r differ by 10\log_{10} r dB, so 20 dB is a factor of 10 in pressure. The sound pressure level is 20\log_{10}(p_{\mathrm{rms}}/20\,\mu\mathrm{Pa}) dB, with p_{\mathrm{rms}} the root-mean-square pressure and 20 μPa about the quietest 1 kHz tone a young listener can hear. Wikipedia: Sound pressure, Decibel

Loudness

A perception: how strong a sound seems, set mainly by the overall size of its partials, its sound pressure level, and by their frequencies (equal-loudness contours). 10 dB more sounds about twice as loud. Wikipedia, and post 1

Equal-loudness contour

A curve giving, for each frequency, the sound pressure level at which a pure tone sounds as loud as a 1 kHz tone at a chosen level. By the standard curves a 100 Hz tone needs about 79 dB to match a 1 kHz tone at 60 dB. Wikipedia, and ISO 226:2023

Attack and decay

The attack is how a sound starts, sudden for a pluck or strike and gradual for a bowed or blown note; the decay is how it fades, each partial shrinking by the factor e in its own fading time. This series counts both as part of timbre. Wikipedia: Envelope (music)

Formant

A band of frequencies that a source’s fixed resonances favor whatever note is played, such as the throat and mouth resonances that set a vowel, or a violin body’s resonances. This series also counts a clarinet’s tone-hole cutoff, roughly 1 to 1.5 kHz, as one. Wikipedia

Timbre

What tells apart two sounds of the same pitch, loudness and length. Writing the sound as p(t) = \sum_n c_n e^{-t/\tau_n}\sin(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n), timbre comes from three things: the ratios c_n/c_1 (bright versus mellow; missing partials), how far the f_n sit from whole-number multiples (smooth, then shimmer, then clang), and how the c_n change over time, especially at the start. Wikipedia, and post 1

Duration

How long a note sounds, set by its fading times \tau_n and by the player, who may damp it (releasing a piano key, a hand on a drumhead) or, on a bowed or blown note, keep it going. Wikipedia: Duration (music)

Fading time

For a partial or mode that fades as e^{-t/\tau}, the time \tau in which it shrinks by the factor e \approx 2.7, a drop of about 8.7 dB. A mode e^{st}W with \operatorname{Re} s < 0 has \tau = -1/\operatorname{Re} s. Wikipedia: Exponential decay

Inharmonic

Having partials that are not whole-number multiples of one frequency. A bell, a drum and a kalimba tine are strongly inharmonic; a piano string is slightly inharmonic. Wikipedia

Note names: C4, A4, middle C

Notes are named by a letter from A to G and an octave number. C4 is middle C, about 262 Hz; C5 is the C an octave above it; A4 is the A at 440 Hz. Wikipedia

Semitone

The smallest step on a piano, from one key to the next, white or black. Twelve semitones make an octave. Wikipedia

Equal temperament

The usual piano tuning, in which every semitone is the ratio 2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595, so twelve make an exact octave. The other intervals then miss the simple ratios slightly: the fifth is 2^{7/12} \approx 1.4983, not 3/2. Wikipedia

Cent

One hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone, so an octave is 1200 cents and two frequencies in the ratio r are 1200\log_2 r cents apart. Trained listeners notice a few cents. Wikipedia

Octave, fifth, twelfth

Intervals named by frequency ratio: the octave is 2, the fifth 3/2 (about 1.498 in equal temperament), and the twelfth, an octave plus a fifth, about 3. The smaller ones by their simple ratios: the minor third 6/5, the major third 5/4, the fourth 4/3 and the major sixth 5/3. Wikipedia

Beats

When two pure tones of nearly equal frequency sound together, their sum swells and fades in loudness at the difference of their frequencies. Tuners listen for beats; fast beats are heard as roughness. Wikipedia

Heterodyning

Making the difference frequency f_1 - f_2 of two signals in a nonlinear circuit, for instance by multiplying them, since \sin(2\pi f_1 t)\sin(2\pi f_2 t) = \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 - f_2)t) - \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 + f_2)t); a theremin makes its tone this way from two radio oscillators. Beats differ: two tones simply added contain no tone at the difference frequency. Wikipedia: Heterodyne, Theremin, and the series index

Consonance, roughness

Consonance is how smooth or stable two notes sound together. Roughness is one ingredient of it: the harsh quality of fast beats between partials that are close but not equal. Wikipedia, and Did instruments shape our scales?

title: Glossary
text:
Instrument parts and playing

Nut, bridge

A string runs between two supports: one on the heavy frame, which barely moves (the nut on a guitar, the capo or agraffe on a piano), and the bridge: on a piano or guitar a hardwood strip glued to the soundboard, on a violin a carved maple piece standing on the top plate, held by the strings’ pressure. After a single pluck or strike the string, with height u(x, t) at position x and time t, pushes the bridge up and down hundreds of times a second, for seconds, with a force set only by its slope at that end, F(t) = -T\,u_x(L, t) for tension T and bridge end x = L, which keeps every frequency and weights each mode by its slope there. On a kalimba, the bridge is the bar the tines are pressed against. Wikipedia

Soundboard

The large thin wooden panel of a piano or guitar to which the bridge is glued. A 1 mm string is too thin to move the air by itself, since air simply flows around it, so the string pushes the bridge, the bridge moves the soundboard, and the soundboard pushes the air. Wikipedia

Impulse response h

On a silent instrument, tap the bridge once, sharply, and record the pressure at your ear per unit of the tap’s strength (force times duration): that recording is h(t). During a note the string’s push F on the bridge is a continuous run of such taps, each heard as a delayed, scaled copy of h, so the pressure is p(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} h(t - s)\,F(s)\,ds; this filter is fixed and linear because small motions obey linear equations, nothing changes in time, and nothing happens before its cause. So p has the same frequencies f_n as the string, once the board’s own ring at the start has died away, each only rescaled, by |H(f_n)| with H the Fourier transform of h, and delayed. Post 2, and Wikipedia

Resonator

An object with resonances: frequencies, near those of its modes, at which it responds strongly when driven. In a bowed or blown instrument it is the string or air column that the bow or breath drives, whose modes decide which partials are strong; a violin’s body is a resonator too. Wikipedia, and post 3

Open string

A string played with no finger pressing it down, so its whole length between the nut and the bridge vibrates. Wikipedia

Harmonics, on a string

Notes a string player gets by touching the string lightly at a fraction of its length, such as the middle, instead of pressing it down. Only the modes with a still point under the finger keep sounding. Wikipedia, and the light touch in post 2

Overblowing, register key

Making a wind instrument’s air column jump to a higher mode. A flutist overblows by blowing faster; a clarinetist presses the register key, which opens a small hole that spoils the lowest mode. Wikipedia, and the clarinet in post 3

Blow, draw

On a harmonica, a blow note sounds when you breathe out through a hole, and a draw note when you breathe in; each hole has one reed for each. Wikipedia

Free reed

A thin metal tongue fixed at one end that swings through a closely fitting slot, opening and shutting it like a valve. Harmonicas and accordions use free reeds. Wikipedia

Damper

A felt pad that stops a piano string when its key is released; the right pedal lifts them all, and roughly the top 20 keys have none. Wikipedia: Sustain pedal

Soft pedal, una corda

The left pedal of a piano. On a grand it shifts the hammers sideways so they hit fewer strings (una corda, “one string”); on an upright it moves them closer to the strings, so they strike more gently. Wikipedia

Practice pedal, mute

The middle pedal on many uprights. It lowers a strip of felt between the hammers and the strings, making the sound much quieter and duller. Wikipedia: Piano pedals

title: Glossary
text:
Grouping instruments

Hornbostel–Sachs classification

The usual scheme for sorting instruments (Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs, 1914), by what makes the sound: idiophones, the body itself (glockenspiel, kalimba); membranophones, a skin (drums); chordophones, strings (violin, piano); aerophones, air (flute, clarinet, harmonica); and, added later, electrophones (theremin). Each class is divided further by decimal codes: the piano is 314.122, a board zither with a resonator box. Wikipedia, and the series index

Operator family

This series’ name for instruments whose operators share one rule up to constants and ends: the violin string and the air in a flute or clarinet share -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, and the kalimba tine, harmonica reed and glockenspiel bar share \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4. Members can still sound different ratios, because the ends are part of each operator, and a family is not a Hornbostel–Sachs class. See the series index.

title: Glossary
text:
Vibration

Partial derivative, u_t, u_{xx}

For a function of several variables, such as a string’s height u(x, t) at position x and time t, the rate of change in one variable with the others held fixed, named by subscripts: u_t is the velocity, u_{tt} the acceleration, u_x the slope and u_{xx}, for small slopes, the curvature. Mixed subscripts mean one derivative after another, in either order for a smooth function: u_{xt} = u_{tx}. Wikipedia

Proportional, \propto

a \propto b means that a is a fixed number times b. So f \propto 1/L^2 means that halving L multiplies f by four. Wikipedia

Angular frequency

\omega = 2\pi f: the frequency counted in radians per second instead of cycles per second. Formulas such as \omega^2 = k/m are shortest in \omega. Wikipedia

Wavenumber

The counterpart of angular frequency in space: a wave \sin kx has wavenumber k = 2\pi/\text{wavelength}. For the wave equation, \omega = ck. Wikipedia

Linear

An equation is linear when it is built from u and its derivatives only by multiplying each by a number or a given function and adding (no u^2, u\,u_x or \sin u), so that sums and multiples of solutions without an outside force are again solutions. The operators of this series are linear; what keeps a bowed string or a reed going is not. Wikipedia

First-order approximation

Keeping only the terms proportional to a small change and dropping its square and higher powers: for small \varepsilon, (1 + \varepsilon)^3 \approx 1 + 3\varepsilon. Wikipedia

Linearization

Replacing a force by its first-order part, accurate for small motions: a pendulum’s restoring force mg\sin\theta becomes mg\,\theta. The result is a linear equation, whose frequencies do not depend on the size of the motion. Wikipedia, and post 2

Superposition

Adding solutions of a linear equation to get another solution. The free motion of a modal instrument is a superposition, a sum, of its modes. Wikipedia

Mode, normal mode 

A motion an object makes on its own, with nothing driving it, in which every part follows one time course, one frequency (or none) and one rate of fading; precisely, for a linear system U' = BU, a nonzero solution e^{st}W, which exists exactly when BW = sW. A normal mode is the frictionless kind, a fixed shape X swinging as \cos(\omega t + \varphi)X, which for u'' = -Au exists exactly when AX = \omega^2X (the appendix). Wikipedia

Complex mode

A mode whose parts swing at one frequency and fade at one rate but peak at different moments: the entries of W in e^{st}W have different phases. They appear with friction that the frictionless modes do not split, such as two slightly mistuned piano strings on one bridge (the appendix). NASA NESC: Complex modes in lightly damped structural systems

Standing wave

A wave whose shape stays in place, such as a mode of a string. It can be seen as two equal waves traveling in opposite directions. Wikipedia

Node, antinode, nodal line

A node is a point of a standing wave that does not move, and an antinode one that moves the most. On a drumhead or a plate a mode stays still along whole curves, its nodal lines, where Chladni’s sand collects. Wikipedia

Wave equation

The equation u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} for the height u(x, t) of a stretched string, and its relatives for air in a pipe and for a drumhead. The constant c is the speed at which a bump travels. Wikipedia, and post 2

Membrane

A sheet with no stiffness of its own, stretched with the same tension T per unit length in every direction, like an ideal drumhead. Its small motions obey u_{tt} = c^2\Delta u, with \Delta the Laplacian, c^2 = T/\sigma and \sigma its mass per unit area. Wikipedia: Vibration of a circular membrane, and post 3

Boundary condition

A rule for what happens at the edge of a vibrating object, set by how it is held: a tied string end has u = 0, a clamped bar end u = u_x = 0, and at a pipe’s open end the pressure equals room pressure. Each is either imposed or natural. Wikipedia, and post 2

Dirichlet and Neumann conditions 

A Dirichlet condition fixes the value at the edge, such as u = 0 at a string’s tied end or p = 0 at a pipe’s open end. A Neumann condition fixes the slope out of the edge, such as p_x = 0 at a clarinet’s nearly closed reed end, where the air cannot move. Wikipedia: Dirichlet, Neumann

Imposed and natural boundary conditions 

An imposed condition restricts the allowed shapes, and the holder enforces it with whatever force it takes, like a clamp’s u = u_x = 0. A natural condition restricts no shape; the motion obeys it because no force acts where nothing holds the object, like a free bar end’s u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0, and in the energy form, the Rayleigh quotient, only imposed conditions are required. P. J. Olver, Boundary conditions and null Lagrangians in the calculus of variations and elasticity, and post 3

End correction

The amount by which an open pipe acts longer than it is, about 0.6 of its radius beyond a bare open end, because the air just outside the end moves with the air inside. Frequencies computed with p = 0 exactly at the end come out slightly too high without it. Wikipedia, J. Wolfe, UNSW: Pipes and harmonics, and post 3

Damping

Friction that drains energy from a vibration, so that it dies away. A term b\,u_t in the equation, proportional to velocity, is the simplest model. Wikipedia

Critical damping

The friction at which a mass on a spring, released, returns to rest fastest without swinging past it: \gamma^2 = 4\lambda in u'' + \gamma u' + \lambda u = 0. Its solutions (a + bt)\,e^{-\gamma t/2} are not combinations of modes, the sign of a Jordan block. Wikipedia: Damping, and the appendix

Internal friction

Energy lost inside a material as it bends or stretches, turned into heat on every swing. With losses to the supports and to radiation, it is one of the three ways a vibrating object loses energy. Wikipedia: Anelasticity, and post 2

Radiation, as a loss

The energy a vibrating object loses to the sound it makes, which is how we hear it and also damps it; shapes that push the air one way over a wide area, like a drumhead’s round modes, radiate strongly and fade fast. Because the sound carries energy into unbounded air, radiation makes the problem no longer self-adjoint (the appendix). D. A. Russell, Sound fields radiated by simple sources; N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapters 7 and 18; the drums in post 3

Self-sustained oscillation, limit cycle 

An oscillation kept at a steady size by a steady supply of energy, such as a bow drawn at constant speed or a steady breath, through a mechanism that is not linear. It settles into one repeating cycle, a limit cycle, from any start near it, and in simple models such as the van der Pol oscillator from any start except complete rest. Wikipedia

Softening and stiffening 

In a softening system the restoring force grows less than in proportion to the displacement, so wider swings are slower, as for a pendulum; in a stiffening one it grows more, so wider swings are faster, as for a string or drumhead swung wide, whose average tension rises. Either way the frequency moves with the size of the motion, which in a linear system it cannot. Wikipedia: Duffing equation, and the appendix

Coupling

Two vibrating parts are coupled when the motion of one pushes on the other, as when piano strings share a bridge. Coupled parts trade energy, and their modes mix. Wikipedia

Parametric resonance

Growth of a vibration when a property such as its stiffness is changed back and forth periodically, most strongly at about twice its natural frequency, as when a child pumps a swing. The simplest model, x'' = -(1 + \varepsilon\cos 2t)\,x for a small number \varepsilon, has no fixed modes. Wikipedia: Parametric oscillator

Floquet theory

The theory of linear equations whose coefficients repeat in time with some period P, such as Mathieu’s x'' = -(1 + \varepsilon\cos 2t)\,x with P = \pi. Floquet’s theorem (1883): when the map from the state at time 0 to the state at time P has distinct eigenvalues, every solution is a combination of e^{\mu t}p(t) with p of period P, and an exponent \mu with positive real part means growth. Wikipedia, and the appendix

Added mass

The extra inertia of a vibrating surface that must push the surrounding air or water along with it, which lowers its frequencies. On a timpani head it lowers the coarsest shapes the most (the drums in post 3). Wikipedia

Helmholtz motion

The way a bowed string moves. The string sticks to the bow, slips back, and sticks again; seen from the side, a single sharp corner races back and forth along the string, one round trip per period. J. Wolfe, UNSW: The bowed string

Clamped, free and pinned ends   

Three ways of holding the end of a bar: a clamped end can neither move nor tilt, u = u_x = 0 (a kalimba tine’s base); a free end carries no bending moment or shear force, u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 (its tip); a pinned end is held in place but free to pivot, u = u_{xx} = 0 (close to a piano string’s ends). The same bar sounds 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 clamped at one end and free at the other, and 1 : 2.76 : 5.40 free at both. Wikipedia: Euler–Bernoulli beam theory, and post 3

Cantilever, clamped bar

A bar fixed rigidly at one end and free at the other, like a diving board. A kalimba tine, pressed against a bridge near one end, is close to one. Wikipedia

Neutral axis

The line along a bent bar that keeps its length, between the stretched outside and the compressed inside of the curve. For a bar of one material it runs through the middle of each cross-section. Wikipedia, and post 3

Euler–Bernoulli beam

The standard model of a bending bar under no tension, \mu u_{tt} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}, with \mu the mass per unit length, E the Young’s modulus and I the second moment of area. Bending is curvature, two derivatives, and balancing forces along the bar adds two more. Wikipedia

Bending moment, shear force

Cut a bent bar at some point: the bending moment is the turning effect one side exerts on the other, and the shear force is the sideways force across the cut. A free end carries neither. Wikipedia: Bending moment, Shear force

Young’s modulus

How stiff a material is when stretched: the force per unit area needed, divided by the fraction by which it lengthens. Steel is about 200 GPa; nylon, used for classical guitar strings, is a few GPa. Wikipedia

Second moment of area

How the shape of a bar’s cross-section resists bending, written I. For a rectangle of width w and thickness h, I = wh^3/12: doubling the thickness makes the bar eight times harder to bend. Wikipedia

Hyperbolic functions, cosh and sinh

\cosh x = (e^x + e^{-x})/2 and \sinh x = (e^x - e^{-x})/2, with \cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1, (\cosh x)' = \sinh x and (\sinh x)' = \cosh x. In a bar they describe bending that grows or fades along the bar instead of wiggling. Wikipedia

Bulk modulus, adiabatic

How hard a material is to compress: the pressure needed, divided by the fraction by which the volume shrinks. A sound wave’s squeezes are too quick for heat to flow (adiabatic), which for air gives about 1.4 \times atmospheric pressure. Wikipedia

Capacitance

How much charge a capacitor holds per volt across it, C = q/V, in farads. In a circuit of a coil and a capacitor, 1/C plays the part of a spring’s stiffness. Wikipedia, and post 3

Inductance

How strongly a coil opposes a change in the current through it: V = L\,dI/dt, measured in henries. In a circuit of a coil and a capacitor, L plays the part of a mass. Wikipedia, and post 3

title: Glossary
text:
Matrices and operators

Matrix times vector

For a square matrix K and a list of numbers v, the product Kv is the list whose j-th entry is \sum_k K_{jk}v_k: row j of K, multiplied entry by entry with v and added up. Wikipedia

Eigenvector, eigenvalue

A nonzero vector v that a matrix K only rescales, Kv = \lambda v; the number \lambda is its eigenvalue. For two beads on a tied string the eigenvectors are (1, 1) and (1, -1), and for this series’ operators an eigenvalue is a squared angular frequency, \lambda = \omega^2 (the appendix). Wikipedia

Eigenvalue

See eigenvector.

Multiplicity

The number of independent eigenvectors, none a combination of the others, that share one eigenvalue. On a ring, the cosine and sine shapes of one wave give their frequency multiplicity 2. Wikipedia

Perpendicular, orthogonal

Two vectors are perpendicular, or orthogonal, when their dot product, the sum of the products of matching entries, is zero. For functions the dot product is replaced by the inner product. Wikipedia

Basis

A set of directions from which every vector can be built in exactly one way by adding multiples of them, such as (1, 1)/\sqrt2 and (1, -1)/\sqrt2 in the plane. The modes of a vibrating object play the same role for its shapes. Wikipedia

Orthonormal

A set of vectors each perpendicular to the others and of length 1, such as (1, 1)/\sqrt2 and (1, -1)/\sqrt2. In an orthonormal basis X_1, X_2, \dots, the amount of X_i in a vector x is the dot product X_i \cdot x. Wikipedia

Symmetric matrix

A square matrix of real numbers whose entry in row i, column j equals the entry in row j, column i. By the spectral theorem its eigenvalues are real and it has a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors. Wikipedia

Diagonalizable

A square matrix B is diagonalizable when it has a basis of eigenvectors W_1, \dots, W_n, complex numbers allowed, so that B = W\operatorname{diag}(s_1, \dots, s_n)\,W^{-1} with W the matrix of the W_k and s_k their eigenvalues. For u'' = -Au, the generator is diagonalizable exactly when A is diagonalizable and invertible (the appendix). Wikipedia

Jordan block

A square matrix with one number s down its diagonal, 1 just above it and 0 elsewhere, such as \left(\begin{smallmatrix} s & 1 \\ 0 & s \end{smallmatrix}\right): the smallest way for a matrix to lack a basis of eigenvectors. For U' = BU a block of size 2 gives the solutions (a + bt)\,e^{st}, which are not combinations of modes: a rigid drift (s = 0) or critical damping. Wikipedia: Jordan normal form

Commuting matrices

Two square matrices commute when AC = CA; a multiple of the identity commutes with every matrix, and C = \alpha + \beta A commutes with A. Two symmetric matrices that commute share an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, which is why friction that commutes with A keeps the frictionless mode shapes (the appendix). Wikipedia

Determinant

A number computed from a square matrix that is zero exactly when the matrix sends some nonzero vector to zero; for rows (p, q) and (r, s) it is ps - qr. So linear equations with zero right-hand sides have a nonzero solution exactly when the determinant of their coefficients is zero. Wikipedia

Circulant matrix

A square matrix in which each row is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around. The complex waves e^{2\pi ijk/N} are eigenvectors of every circulant, and of a symmetric one, such as beads closed into a ring, so are the real cosine and sine waves. Wikipedia

Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)

Writing a list of N numbers, indexed by j = 0, \dots, N-1, as a sum of the waves \cos(2\pi jk/N) and \sin(2\pi jk/N) for k = 0, \dots, N-1, or with Euler’s formula of e^{2\pi ijk/N}. Wikipedia

Euler’s formula

e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta, where i^2 = -1. It packs a cosine and a sine into one expression that is easier to multiply and differentiate. Wikipedia

Operator

For an object held in a given way, the linear map, defined on the shapes the holding allows, that sends a shape to minus the acceleration it causes, so the free motion obeys u_{tt} = -Au; for a string of tension T and mass \mu per length, A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 with c^2 = T/\mu, on shapes that are zero at both ends. Each eigenvalue \lambda of A gives a frequency \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi. Wikipedia, and post 2

Generator

For a linear equation U' = BU that does not change in time, the matrix or operator B, which turns the state U into its rate of change; for u'' = -Au the state is U = (u, u') and B = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & I \\ -A & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right). The solutions are U(t) = e^{tB}U(0), which is why B is said to generate them. Wikipedia: Matrix exponential, and the appendix

Modal system

This series’ term for a linear system U' = BU whose modes form a basis of its states (in infinite dimensions, a Riesz basis of the energy space), so that every motion is a sum of modes. Two beads on a tied string are modal; closed into a ring, which can drift, they are not (the appendix).

Eigenfunction

A nonzero function f that an operator only rescales: Af = \lambda f. Example: -\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\cos 3\theta = 9\cos 3\theta. Wikipedia

Spectrum

For this series’ instruments, the list of the operator’s eigenvalues \lambda, each giving a frequency \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi that passes unchanged into the sound; in general, the set of numbers z for which A - z has no bounded inverse. An infinite string has the continuous spectrum [0, \infty) and no eigenvalues, and for a self-adjoint A \ge 0 the spectrum is a list exactly when the resolvent is compact. Wikipedia, and the appendix

Inner product

A way to multiply two vectors or two functions to get a number, generalizing the dot product: for functions on the circle, \langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,\bar g\,d\theta, with \bar g the complex conjugate of g. Two functions are perpendicular if it is zero. Wikipedia

L^2(S^1)

The space of functions on the circle S^1 with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta finite, with the inner product above (functions that differ only on a set of measure zero count as the same). It is where the shapes of a vibrating loop live. Wikipedia

Symmetric and self-adjoint operators

An operator A is symmetric if \langle Af, g\rangle = \langle f, Ag\rangle for all allowed f and g, which makes its eigenvalues real and its eigenfunctions for different eigenvalues perpendicular. Self-adjoint, A = A^* with domains included, is a stronger condition on the allowed shapes; with a compact resolvent it gives enough eigenfunctions to build every shape (the appendix). Wikipedia

Fourier series

Writing a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines, or of e^{in\theta}, of whole-number frequencies. In the appendix it is the expansion in the modes of the loop of string. Wikipedia

Laplacian

The operator \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} in the plane; at each point it is proportional to how far u sits below the average of its values on a small circle around the point. A drumhead’s operator is -c^2\Delta. Wikipedia

Separation of variables

Looking for solutions that are a fixed shape times a function of time, u(x, t) = X(x)\,q(t). Putting this into u_{tt} = -Au gives q''X = -q\,AX, so such a motion exists exactly when AX = \lambda X for a number \lambda, and then q'' = -\lambda q, a spring. Wikipedia

Bessel function

The functions J_m(r) that describe how a round drum’s modes vary from the center to the rim, as sines do along a string. Their zeros, 2.405, 5.520, 8.654, \dots for J_0, are not whole-number multiples of the first one, and set the drum’s frequencies. Wikipedia, and the drums in post 3

Divergence theorem

The total flow out through the boundary of a region equals the sum, over the region, of how much flow is created at each point. It turns forces along the edge of a patch of drumhead into an integral over the patch. Wikipedia

Rayleigh quotient

A shape’s stored energy divided by its mass-weighted size, such as R(X) = \int T\,(X')^2\,dx \big/ \int \mu\,X^2\,dx for a string; at a mode it equals the eigenvalue \lambda, and its smallest value over the shapes that obey the imposed end conditions is the lowest eigenvalue. It explains why removing metal near the base of a reed or tine lowers its pitch and removing it near the tip raises it. Wikipedia

Min–max principle

List the eigenvalues in order, \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots; then \lambda_n is the least, over all n-dimensional families of allowed shapes, of the largest Rayleigh quotient in the family (the Courant–Fischer theorem). So added stiffness never lowers an eigenvalue, added mass never raises one, and holding the object more firmly never lowers one. Wikipedia, and the appendix

title: Glossary
text:
The deeper theory

Resolvent

For an operator A and a number z, the inverse (A - z)^{-1}, when it exists and is bounded: the operator that solves Au - zu = f for u. The numbers z at which it fails to exist are the spectrum. Wikipedia: Resolvent formalism

Compact operator, compact resolvent 

An operator on a Hilbert space is compact when it is a limit, in the operator norm, of operators whose outputs fill only finitely many dimensions; every matrix is compact. An operator A has compact resolvent when (A - z)^{-1} is compact, and for self-adjoint A \ge 0 this holds exactly when the spectrum is a list \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots \to \infty of finite multiplicity with an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, as for strings, bars and drums of finite size. Wikipedia: Compact operator on Hilbert space, and the appendix

Green’s function, Green’s operator

For a linear problem Au = f with boundary conditions, the Green’s function G(x, y) is the response at x to a unit point load at y, and the Green’s operator f \mapsto \int G(x, y)\,f(y)\,dy is A^{-1} written as an integral. For the bar its kernel is continuous on the square [0, L]^2, which makes it compact (the appendix). Wikipedia

Functional calculus

A way to apply a function \varphi of numbers to an operator: for a symmetric matrix with orthonormal eigenvectors X_i and eigenvalues \lambda_i, \varphi(A)f = \sum_i \varphi(\lambda_i)\,(X_i\cdot f)\,X_i, and von Neumann’s spectral theorem does the same for a self-adjoint operator. It lets the appendix write every motion of u'' = -Au as \cos(t\sqrt A)\,f + \big(\sin(t\sqrt A)/\sqrt A\big)\,g. Wikipedia: Borel functional calculus

Semigroup

For U' = BU, the operators e^{tB}, t \ge 0, each sending a starting state to the state at time t, with e^{0B} = I and e^{(t + t')B} = e^{tB}e^{t'B}. For an unbounded generator such as a damped string’s, semigroup theory (the Hille–Yosida and Lumer–Phillips theorems) builds e^{tB} directly, proving that every start has exactly one motion whether or not there are enough modes. Wikipedia: C0-semigroup

Riesz basis

A basis of a Hilbert space that behaves like an orthonormal one up to fixed factors: every vector is uniquely U = \sum_k c_kW_k with m\sum_k|c_k|^2 \le \|U\|^2 \le M\sum_k|c_k|^2 for fixed 0 < m \le M. A set can be complete, with no nonzero vector perpendicular to all of it, and still fail to be a Riesz basis. Encyclopedia of Mathematics, and the appendix

Normal and non-normal

A matrix B is normal when it commutes with its adjoint, BB^* = B^*B, and exactly then it has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. A non-normal matrix may be diagonalizable with nearly parallel eigenvectors, so that decaying modes nearly cancel at the start and the motion grows for a while before it decays. Wikipedia: Normal matrix, and the appendix

Pseudospectrum

For a matrix B and a small \varepsilon > 0, the set of numbers z with \|(B - z)^{-1}\| > 1/\varepsilon, equivalently the eigenvalues of all B + E with \|E\| < \varepsilon. For a non-normal B it can reach far beyond the spectrum, measuring behaviour such as growth before decay (Trefethen and Embree). Wikipedia

title: Glossary
text:
Shape and spectrum

Weyl’s law

For a drum of area |\Omega|, the number N(\Lambda) of eigenvalues of -\Delta below a large number \Lambda is close to |\Omega|\Lambda/4\pi, so the area can be heard. A second term, -P\sqrt\Lambda/4\pi with P the perimeter, is proved only under extra conditions, but for smooth or polygonal rims the perimeter can be heard anyway (Can you hear the shape of a drum?). Wikipedia

Isospectral

Having the same spectrum, counted with multiplicity. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert found two differently shaped drums that are isospectral. Wikipedia: Hearing the shape of a drum

title: What you hear
text:
The Shape of a Sound · 2 · One string, end to end → · Glossary
A sound has a clear pitch when its partials, the pure tones it is made of, sit at or very near whole-number multiples of one frequency. A plucked string’s partials do, so it gives a note you could hum; a struck drum’s don’t, so it gives a thud.
The reason: partials on the multiples of one frequency add up to a sound that repeats at that rate, and the ear hears the repetition rate as the pitch.

title: What you hear
text:
Four aspects of a sound
We hear four things in a sound: pitch, loudness, timbre and duration. They are perceptions, measured by asking listeners,1 and each comes from different numbers in one formula for the sound.
1 B. C. J. Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., Emerald, Bingley, 2012 (reissued by Brill, Leiden, 2013), chapters 4, 6 and 8 (loudness, pitch, timbre); R. Plomp, Aspects of Tone Sensation: A Psychophysical Study, Academic Press, 1976.Sound is the air pressure p(t) at your ear at time t, measured from the average air pressure. An instrument plucked or struck and then left to ring sounds, to a good approximation, 
p(t) = \sum_n c_n e^{-t/\tau_n}\sin(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n).
 Term n is a partial: a pure tone, like a tuning fork’s, with frequency f_n in hertz (cycles per second), numbered from the lowest, starting size c_n and phase \varphi_n, the point in its cycle where it starts. It shrinks by a factor of e \approx 2.7 every \tau_n seconds, its fading time. Each partial comes from one of the instrument’s modes, a shape the object swings in at one frequency. A bowed or blown note is the same sum without the fading, for as long as the player keeps going (route 4 below).
The four aspects come from these numbers:

Pitch, how high or low the sound is, comes from the f_n: the pitch is the largest frequency of which they are all (nearly) whole-number multiples; often f_1, but not when the common frequency is missing (below).
Loudness, how strong it seems, comes from the overall size of the c_n.
Timbre, what tells apart two sounds of the same pitch, loudness and length,2 comes from three things:

the ratios c_n/c_1 (bright versus mellow; missing partials);
how far the f_n sit from whole-number multiples (smooth, then shimmer, then clang);
how each partial’s size changes over time, especially at the start.3

Duration comes from the \tau_n, and from the player’s damping.

2 Adapted from the ANSI/ASA definition of timbre (terminology 12.09), which names loudness and pitch, as quoted by Wikipedia, Timbre.3 Wikipedia, Timbre; Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 8.
Pitch
Pitch is measured as the frequency of the pure tone that listeners match a sound to.4 Pitch that can carry a melody is heard from about 30 Hz5 up to about 4 or 5 kHz for pure tones;6 call this the range we hear as pitch. The partials at 1, 2, 3, … times a frequency are its harmonics.
4 Acoustical Society of America, Standard terminology: pitch, 11.01; Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 6, for the definition by matching to a pure tone.5 D. Pressnitzer, R. D. Patterson and K. Krumbholz, The lower limit of melodic pitch, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 109 (2001), 2074–2084.6 A. J. Oxenham, C. Micheyl, M. V. Keebler, A. Loper and S. Santurette, Pitch perception beyond the traditional existence region of pitch, PNAS 108(18) (2011), 7629–7634.

  ▶ Pure tone, 220 Hz▶ Partials at 220, 440, 660, … Hz▶ Pure tone, 440 Hz
  The second sound has ten partials, at 1, 2, …, 10 times 220 Hz, with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/10. It sounds richer than the first and just as high, so its pitch is 220 Hz. The third is an octave higher.




Loudness
Loudness is set mainly by the sound pressure level: 10 dB more is ten times the power and sounds about twice as loud.7 At the same level, a low tone sounds quieter than a mid-range one.8
7 S. S. Stevens, “On the psychophysical law”, Psychological Review 64 (1957), 153–181; Wikipedia, Sone (twice as loud per 10 dB) and Stevens’s power law.8 ISO 226:2023, Acoustics — Normal equal-loudness-level contours; HyperPhysics, Equal loudness curves.


DetailsDecibels, equal-loudness contours and the power law

The sound pressure level is 20\log_{10}(p_{\mathrm{rms}}/20\,\mu\mathrm{Pa}) decibels (dB), where p_{\mathrm{rms}}, the root-mean-square pressure, is the square root of the long-run average of p(t)^2. For steady partials, p_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 = \tfrac12\sum_n c_n^2, by the averages in the proof below. The intensity, the power carried through each square metre, grows as p_{\mathrm{rms}}^2, so 10 dB more is ten times the intensity. By the equal-loudness contours of ISO 226, which give the level at which pure tones of each frequency sound equally loud to young listeners, a 100 Hz tone needs about 79 dB to match a 1 kHz tone at 60 dB (ISO 226:2023, Acoustics — Normal equal-loudness-level contours). At equal intensity, partials spread beyond a certain width in frequency sound louder than partials bunched together (E. Zwicker, G. Flottorp and S. S. Stevens, “Critical band width in loudness summation”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 29 (1957), 548–557). Loudness grows roughly as the 0.3 power of intensity, so 10 dB more sounds about twice as loud, since 10^{0.3} \approx 2 (S. S. Stevens, “On the psychophysical law”, Psychological Review 64 (1957), 153–181; Wikipedia, Stevens’s power law).




  Same size of pressure swing:▶ 100 Hz▶ 1000 Hz▶ 3000 Hz▶ All three in turn
  1000 Hz, three levels:▶ 0, then −10, then −20 dB
  First row: three pure tones with the same size of pressure swing; small laptop and phone speakers make the 100 Hz tone sound even quieter than headphones do. Second row: one tone, stepped down 10 dB twice.




Timbre
Timbre also depends on two things the formula leaves out: noise and transients that are not modes, such as bow noise, breath and a hammer’s thump; and fixed resonances that favor the same bands of frequency whatever note is played, such as a violin’s body or a clarinet’s tone-hole cutoff (formants).9
9 M. Schleske, Introduction to violin acoustics: sound, on the violin body’s fixed resonances; E. Moers and J. Kergomard, “On the cutoff frequency of clarinet-like instruments. Geometrical versus acoustical regularity”, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 97 (2011), 984–996 (arXiv:1101.4742), and J. Wolfe and colleagues, Clarinet acoustics: F3, UNSW, on the clarinet’s tone-hole cutoff.


DetailsThe evidence for the start, and the formants

Removing the onsets of recorded instrument tones cut listeners’ accuracy at naming the instruments by about 15 percentage points (E. Saldanha and J. F. Corso, “Timbre cues and the identification of musical instruments”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 36 (1964), 2021–2026, as summarized in K. Siedenburg, Specifying the perceptual relevance of onset transients for musical instrument identification, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 145 (2019), 1078–1087). Listeners also hear a finger hitting a piano key and the key hitting bottom (W. Goebl, R. Bresin and I. Fujinaga, Perception of touch quality in piano tones, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 136 (2014), 2839–2850). A violin’s body favors certain bands of frequency whatever the note, as a voice’s formants do (M. Schleske, Introduction to violin acoustics: sound). Above a cutoff frequency, roughly 1 to 1.5 kHz on a clarinet, sound waves travel on past the open tone holes instead of being turned back by them, and that cutoff depends little on the fingering (E. Moers and J. Kergomard, “On the cutoff frequency of clarinet-like instruments. Geometrical versus acoustical regularity”, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 97 (2011), 984–996, arXiv:1101.4742; J. Wolfe and colleagues, Clarinet acoustics: F3, UNSW).




  ▶ Pure tone▶ Every harmonic▶ Odd harmonics only▶ Every harmonic, plucked
  Four sounds at 220 Hz. The first three are steady, with equal power: one partial; twelve harmonics with sizes 1, 1/2, 1/3, …; and only the odd ones of those, which sounds hollow, like a clarinet. The fourth has the second's partials but starts suddenly and fades, the higher partials faster, like a pluck.


Dynamics change timbre too. A harder piano blow is brighter as well as louder: the hammer’s felt gets harder the more it is squashed, so a fast hammer stays on the string for a shorter time and starts more high partials.10 With a felt that stayed equally soft, a loud note would be a soft note turned up.11
10 A. Askenfelt and E. Jansson, “From touch to string vibrations” (the nonlinear hammer; string contact), in Five Lectures on the Acoustics of the Piano, Royal Swedish Academy of Music, 1990.11 D. A. Russell, Hammer nonlinearity, dynamics and the piano sound, 1997.

  ▶ Soft blow▶ Hard blow▶ Soft blow, turned up
  Middle C on a model piano string. The third button plays the soft blow 10 dB louder, at the hard blow's average level, and it still sounds duller. How fast the partials fall off with number is illustrative, not computed from a model of the felt.




Duration
A ringing note lasts as long as its fading times allow, unless the player damps it: a key released, a mute, a hand on a drumhead, or a bass drummer’s leg or towel.12
12 “How to play the bass drum properly”, with Keith Aleo, Interlochen Center for the Arts, 3 April 2023.

  Plucked:▶ Let it ring▶ Damp it after 0.35 s
  Bowed:▶ Half a second▶ Two seconds
  A string at 196 Hz. Damped, the plucked note's partials all die within about a tenth of a second. Bowed, it is a steady tone, with partials of sizes 1, 1/2, 1/3, …, that lasts as long as the bow moves.

title: What you hear
text:
Why whole numbers repeat
Steady partials add up to a sound that repeats exactly when their frequencies are all whole-number multiples of one frequency. Take two pure tones at 220 and 330 Hz, in the ratio 3 : 2: after two cycles of the lower tone the upper has completed three, so the sum starts again, 110 times a second. At the ratio 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, the sum starts again only after 100 cycles of the lower tone, 2.2 times a second.


  ▶ 2 : 1▶ 3 : 2▶ 1.59 : 1 (a drum)Play the slider's ratio
  Ratio2.00×
  
  
  Two pure tones, the lower at 220 Hz; gray ticks mark its cycles. At 1.59 : 1 the sum lines up only after 100 cycles, far off the right of this picture.


A signal p is periodic with period P > 0 if p(t+P) = p(t) for every t. The repetition rate of a periodic sound is 1 over its shortest period.

Precisely. Let 
p(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} c_n\sin(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n),
 with distinct frequencies f_n > 0 and sizes c_n \ne 0. A time P > 0 is a period of p exactly when every f_nP is a whole number. So p is periodic exactly when every ratio f_n/f_1 is a fraction, and then its shortest period is 1/g, where g is the largest frequency of which every f_n is a whole-number multiple; its repetition rate is g.




ProofSinusoids of different frequencies are independent, so a period must fit every partial integrals of products of sines and cosines, and divisibility

Lemma. Let 0 < g_1 < \dots < g_m, and suppose that \sum_{j=1}^m \big(\alpha_j\cos(2\pi g_j t) + \beta_j\sin(2\pi g_j t)\big) = 0 for every t. Then every \alpha_j and \beta_j is 0.
Proof of the lemma. For a function w, write \langle w\rangle = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T} w(t)\,dt for its long-run average, when the limit exists. For \gamma \ne 0, \int_{-T}^{T}\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\,dt = \sin(2\pi\gamma T)/(\pi\gamma) stays bounded as T grows, so \langle\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\rangle = 0; and \langle 1\rangle = 1. The product formulas 2\cos x\cos y = \cos(x-y) + \cos(x+y) and 2\sin x\sin y = \cos(x-y) - \cos(x+y) then give, for a, b > 0, \langle\cos(2\pi a t)\cos(2\pi b t)\rangle = \langle\sin(2\pi a t)\sin(2\pi b t)\rangle = \tfrac12 if a = b and 0 if a \ne b. A product of a sine and a cosine is an odd function, so its integral over [-T, T] is 0, and so is its average. Multiply the assumed identity by \cos(2\pi g_j t) and average: every term vanishes except \alpha_j/2, by the averages just computed, so \alpha_j = 0. Multiplying by \sin(2\pi g_j t) gives \beta_j = 0 in the same way.
Proof of the statement. If every f_nP is a whole number, each sine completes whole cycles in time P, so p(t + P) = p(t). Conversely, suppose p(t+P) = p(t) for every t. By the identity \sin(\theta + \delta) - \sin\theta = 2\sin(\delta/2)\cos(\theta + \delta/2), with \theta = 2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n and \delta = 2\pi f_n P, 
0 = p(t+P) - p(t) = \sum_{n=1}^N 2c_n\sin(\pi f_nP)\,\cos\!\big(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n + \pi f_nP\big).
 Expanding each term into \alpha_n\cos(2\pi f_n t) + \beta_n\sin(2\pi f_n t) gives \alpha_n^2 + \beta_n^2 = 4c_n^2\sin^2(\pi f_nP). The lemma makes every \alpha_n and \beta_n zero, so c_n\sin(\pi f_nP) = 0; since c_n \ne 0 by hypothesis, \sin(\pi f_n P) = 0, which means f_nP is a whole number. This proves the first sentence.
The shortest period. If p has a period P, the first sentence makes every f_nP a whole number, so f_n/f_1 = (f_nP)/(f_1P) is a fraction. Conversely, suppose every f_n/f_1 is a fraction. Over a common denominator D, f_n = q_n h with h = f_1/D and whole numbers q_n. Let d be the greatest common divisor of q_1, \dots, q_N and g = dh; then f_n = m_ng with whole numbers m_n = q_n/d whose greatest common divisor is 1. By the first sentence, P is a period exactly when every m_n\,gP is a whole number. If gP is a whole number, so is every m_n\,gP. Conversely, Bézout’s identity (whole numbers whose greatest common divisor is 1 have a combination with whole-number coefficients equal to 1) gives whole numbers u_n with \sum_n u_nm_n = 1, so gP = \sum_n u_n\,(m_n\,gP) is a whole number. So the periods are exactly the whole-number multiples of 1/g, and the shortest is 1/g. Finally, if every f_n is a whole-number multiple of some g', then 1/g' is a period, hence a multiple of 1/g, so g' \le g: g is the largest such frequency.
Check on the examples. Partials at 440, 660 and 880 Hz have h = 220, q_n = 2, 3, 4 and d = 1, so g = 220 Hz although no partial sits there. Tones at 100 and 159 Hz have g = 1 Hz: the sum repeats once a second.


Real partials fade, or sit only near the multiples, so the sound only nearly repeats. Its repetition rate is then the largest frequency g in the range we hear as pitch such that every strong partial lies within a set tolerance of a whole-number multiple of g. The tolerance comes from hearing: a low partial mistuned by more than about 1 to 3%, depending on the listener, stands out as a separate tone.13 Within 2%, the drum’s strong partials in the first demo fit no g above about 20 Hz, below the range we hear as pitch; the string’s fit 196 Hz exactly.
13 B. C. J. Moore, B. R. Glasberg and R. W. Peters, Thresholds for hearing mistuned partials as separate tones in harmonic complexes, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 80 (1986), 479–483; Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 3, on hearing out partials.


PreciselyThe drum’s fit at each tolerance, and fading sounds

Take the partials of the drum in the first demo up to 3.2 times the lowest that start with at least a tenth of the strongest one’s size: 1, 1.593, 2.295, 2.653 and 3.155 times 140 Hz. (Its partials at 2.136 and 2.917 start at only about 2% of the strongest’s size, because the strike point or the listening point sits near a still line of their modes.) Call a frequency g a fit within a tolerance \epsilon if each partial lies within the fraction \epsilon of a whole-number multiple kg with k \ge 1. A computer search over g gives the largest fit; adding the drum’s higher partials could only lower it.



Tolerance
Largest fit g




1%
about 14 Hz


2%
about 20 Hz


3%
about 46 Hz



Within 3%, a base of about 46 Hz fits, as its 3rd, 5th, 7th, 8th and 10th multiples, with nothing at the base or at its 2nd or 4th multiple. That tolerance is generous: the thresholds above are for one mistuned partial among exact harmonics, and here every partial is off at once. In the first demo the sound is a thud.
Fading sounds. A sound that dies away cannot repeat exactly: if p(t+P) = p(t) for every t, then p(t) = p(t + rP) for every whole number r, which tends to 0 as r grows, so p is zero. It can nearly repeat: if every partial sits on a multiple of g and fades with the same time \tau, each period is the one before shrunk by the factor e^{-1/(g\tau)}, by 0.45% at g = 220 Hz and \tau = 1 s.

title: What you hear
text:
The missing fundamental
The pitch of a single note (not a chord) is its repetition rate, even when no partial sits there;14 call this the pitch rule.
14 Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 6.

  
    ▶ The note▶ Without its 220 Hz partial
    Play again
  
  
  
  
  Mix your own
    Pure toneHollow, like a clarinet
    
  
  The wave over three cycles of 220 Hz, each marked by a gray tick, and its partials on the pitch ruler. The readout gives the repetition rate.


Remove its 220 Hz partial (second button): the wave changes shape but still repeats every 1/220 of a second, and the pitch stays. Hearing the pitch with no partial at the repetition rate, the fundamental, is the missing-fundamental effect; it keeps a deep voice’s pitch over a telephone line, which carries little below about 300 Hz.15 In “Mix your own”, keep only 2×, 4×, 6× and 8×, and the pitch jumps an octave.
15 Wikipedia, Missing fundamental.
Beats
Two partials close in frequency are heard as one tone that swells and fades. For two equal pure tones at f_1 and f_2, 
\sin(2\pi f_1 t) + \sin(2\pi f_2 t) = 2\cos\big(\pi (f_2 - f_1) t\big)\,\sin\big(\pi (f_1 + f_2) t\big),
 a tone at the average frequency whose size swells and fades |f_2 - f_1| times a second: beats.16 Faster beats sound rough, and tones far enough apart sound as two smooth tones.17
16 Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 1.17 R. Plomp and W. J. M. Levelt, Tonal consonance and critical bandwidth, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 38 (1965), 548–560.

  ▶ 220 + 222 Hz▶ 220 + 228 Hz▶ 220 + 245 Hz▶ 220 + 330 Hz
  
  
  The sum of two equal pure tones over one second. At 110 Hz apart the swells come too fast to see here, and you hear two smooth tones.




Exceptions to the pitch rule
The pitch rule fails for three kinds of sound.
Chords. C4 and G4 (note names) tuned to exactly 3 : 2 together repeat 130.8 times a second, the rate of C3, yet you hear two notes: the ear sorts the partials into two sets of harmonics, with different bases, and hears each set as one sound.18
18 A. S. Bregman, Auditory Scene Analysis: The Perceptual Organization of Sound, MIT Press, 1990; and his page Introduction to auditory scene analysis.

  ▶ C4▶ G4▶ C4 and G4 together▶ C3, the pair's repetition rate
  Each note has eight harmonics, with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/8: C4 at 261.6 Hz, G4 at exactly 3/2 of that, 392.4 Hz.


Bells and kettledrums. A harmonic subset of the partials sets the pitch, and the ear may choose an octave above that subset’s base. A bell is heard roughly an octave below its main partial, the nominal, often with no partial at the pitch heard.19 A kettledrum is named an octave above the base its main partials fit.20
19 W. A. Hibbert, What note do we hear when a bell rings?20 HyperPhysics, The Timpani, tabulating A. H. Benade, Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics, Oxford University Press, 1976.21 J. Jaatinen and J. Pätynen, Effect of inharmonicity on pitch perception and subjective tuning of piano tones, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 152 (2022), 1146–1157.Strongly stretched partials. Partials running sharp of the multiples, as on a stiff piano string, pull the pitch up.21



DetailsThe bell’s and the kettledrum’s partials

The bell. In a well-tuned church bell the main partials, the hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal, sit near 0.5, 1, 1.2, 1.5 and 2 times the prime, and two more, the superquint and the octave nominal, near 3 and 4 times (W. A. Hibbert, The upper partials of bells). The nominal, superquint and octave nominal, nearly in the ratios 2 : 3 : 4, are heard as harmonics of a missing fundamental, the strike note: the pitch the bell is heard at, roughly an octave below the nominal and close to the prime (W. A. Hibbert, The strike note of bells, first published in The Ringing World, 20 June 2003, p. 586; Wikipedia, Strike tone). It can differ from half the nominal by about a quarter of a semitone, and often no partial sits exactly at it (W. A. Hibbert, What note do we hear when a bell rings?). Measured from the hum, the main partials sit at 1, 2, 2.4, 3, 4, 6 and 8: whole numbers, except the tierce, a minor third above the prime. Without the tierce they fit the hum as base, yet the bell is heard an octave higher.
The kettledrum. A kettledrum’s air pulls one set of its modes near 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a base, yet players name the note an octave higher, at the lowest of the set, the drum’s principal tone. A kettledrum measured by Benade, tuned to C3, had its principal tone at 130.8 Hz and partials at about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times it, close to 3, 4, 5 and 6 times half of it, together with others off this pattern (HyperPhysics, The Timpani, tabulating A. H. Benade, Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics, Oxford University Press, 1976). So the set forms a near-harmonic series on C2, 65.4 Hz, yet the drum is named for its principal tone, C3. The drum’s many partials off whole-number ratios make its exact pitch hard to pin down (Institute of Musical Acoustics (Wiener Klangstil), University of Music and Performing Arts Vienna, The Viennese timpani).

title: What you hear
section: Four routes to a clear pitch
text:
Four routes to a clear pitch
Instruments reach a clear pitch by four routes: modes on the whole numbers by nature, modes moved there by design, off-line partials suppressed, or a drive that repeats.
1×2×3×

By nature: strings and air columns. A string’s n-th mode fits n half-waves between its ends (the picture), and waves of every length travel along the string at the same speed, so an ideal string’s n-th mode swings at exactly n times the lowest frequency. A flute’s air column, open at both ends, resonates at every whole-number multiple, and a clarinet’s, closed at the reed, at the odd ones.22
By design. A marimba bar’s arch, cut underneath, moves its first overtone from 2.76 times the lowest, for a uniform bar, to 4 times.23 A kettledrum’s air slows its coarse shapes most, pulling one set of modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 (post 3).
By suppression. Some off-line partials die fast: a kalimba tine’s overtones, at 6.27 and 17.55 times its lowest, die within a fraction of a second.24 Others are never started: a strike at a still point of a mode does not set that mode going, and timpanists strike between halfway and three-quarters of the way out,25 near the still lines of several modes that do not fit the note.
By a repeating drive: bow and breath. A bow or a breath keeps feeding the motion, which settles into one repeating cycle, so its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples, whatever the object’s own modes.26 A harmonica reed’s own overtones are off the lines, yet blown it chops the air into identical puffs (post 3). The object’s modes only shape which partials are strong.

22 J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW.23 HyperPhysics, Xylophone and marimba; G. P. Scavone, Percussion instruments, course notes, CCRMA, Stanford University, 1999; N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 19 (bars).24 D. M. F. Chapman, The sound of the African thumb piano (kalimba), Acoustics’08 Paris, paper 5aMUf1, Acoustical Society of America, 2008.25 HyperPhysics, The Timpani (the playing spot).26 J. Wolfe, How harmonic are harmonics?, UNSW. Why whole numbers repeat proves this for a finite sum of partials.

Row 3: a kalimba tine at C5, its overtones fading fast as measured, then the same partials ringing as long as the lowest. Row 4: plucked, the reed has the tine's off-line frequencies; blown, its partials sit at whole-number multiples only.

title: What you hear
text:
Next
As a preview, the f_n and c_n come from the instrument, read back from your ear in three steps. The sound is p = h \ast F: copies of h, the sound at your ear of one sharp tap on the instrument’s body, delayed and scaled by F(t), the force with which the vibrating object pushes the body. The force comes from the object’s motion u, which obeys u_{tt} = -Au, where u_{tt} is its acceleration; the spectrum of the operator A sets the f_n. Post 2 works this chain for the plucked string, post 3 for the other instruments, and the appendix When does an equation have a spectrum? in general.

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← 2 · One string, end to end · Violin → · Glossary
Struck or plucked and left to ring, most instruments sound at the frequencies set by their own eigenvalues: a little sharp of whole-number multiples of the fundamental on a piano, far off them on a kalimba, between them on a drum. Bowed, blown or, like the theremin, kept going by a circuit, they sound exactly on whole-number multiples. Below, one instrument from each of the five Hornbostel–Sachs classes1 plays Grieg,2 every voice built from the spectra on this page.

title: Other instruments, same recipe
section: What you hear: two kinds of instrument
text:
What you hear: two kinds of instrument
What you hear is a sum of partials, {p(t) = \sum_n c_n e^{-t/\tau_n}\sin(2\pi f_nt + \varphi_n)}, read as in post 1, and the instruments come in two kinds by where the frequencies f_n sit.
A ringing instrument is struck or plucked, then left alone: its partials sit at its operator’s spectrum (below), each fading at its own rate.
A self-sustained instrument is kept going by a bow, an air jet, a reed or an amplifier, whose push depends on the motion itself, not in proportion to it.3 The drive locks the motion into one repeating cycle, a self-sustained oscillation, so the frequencies are exact multiples nf_1 of the playing frequency f_1 (post 1). The spectrum of the driven part, the resonator, then decides which notes can sound; the drive’s waveform (on a harmonica, the puff’s shape) and the resonator (and, for the violin, the body) decide how strong each partial is.
3 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapters 10 (bowed strings), 15 (woodwind reed instruments) and 16 (flutes).In every demo the stems are the sound’s partials on post 1’s pitch ruler, whose gray lines are whole-number multiples of one frequency; taller stems are stronger partials.

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
How the sound gets out
The vibrating part pushes on something that moves the air. A string about 1 mm thick is too thin to move the air itself,4 so it pushes the bridge, which moves the soundboard, a large thin wooden panel that pushes the air. A piano’s or guitar’s bridge is glued on; a violin’s is a carved maple piece held on the top plate by the strings’ pressure.5 A kalimba tine pushes its box through the clamp. A drum skin, and the air at a tube’s open end, push the air directly.
4 A. Askenfelt (ed.), Five Lectures on the Acoustics of the Piano, Royal Swedish Academy of Music, 1990, “Introduction”: “as the thin string cannot radiate a sound wave itself”.5 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 10 (bowed string instruments): the violin’s bridge.
piano, guitar, violinstringbridgesoundboardkalimbatineclampboxdrumskinclarinetreedopen end
Each vibrating part drawn in its lowest mode, at two moments. Orange: the push that leaves it. Dashed: the sound going out.

As in post 2, the sound at your ear is p = h * F: the input F that reaches the air, convolved with the tap response h. Once the body’s own ring at the start has died away, this keeps each frequency and multiplies it by |H(f)|, where H is the Fourier transform of h.
The input F comes from the vibrating part’s motion u by a route specific to each instrument, the table’s second row. Each route acts at each instant, so it keeps every frequency and only weights each mode: for a string of tension T and length L, F = -T\,u_x(L, t) weights mode n by T times its end slope, \pm n\pi/L (subscripts are partial derivatives).
In the table, which leaves out fading, a_n and \psi_n are the size and phase of mode n in u, X_n is mode n’s shape (next section), \omega_n = 2\pi f_n, x runs along a string or tube, and u_{tt} is the acceleration.

DetailsWhy the frequencies survive, and the drum, kalimba and clarinet columns

A sine stays a sine. With H(f) = \int h(s)\,e^{-2\pi i f s}\,ds, the Fourier transform of h, a short computation gives h * \sin(\omega t) = |H(f)|\sin(\omega t + \arg H(f)) for \omega = 2\pi f. So with one input, c_n is the input’s amount of mode n times |H(f_n)|.
Drum. A drum small compared with the wavelength sends out sound in proportion to the net volume each mode sweeps, so for a given swing and frequency c_n \propto |\iint X_n\,dA|. A mode with m \ge 1 still lines through the center varies around the drum as \cos m\theta, so \iint X_n\,dA = 0: their sound is zero at this (monopole) order, and they radiate only weakly, as dipoles (m = 1) or weaker, while the round modes radiate strongly (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapters 7 and 18).
Kalimba. The clamp, at x = 0, passes two things to the box: the bent tine’s shear force, F_1 = V(0, t) = -EI\,u_{xxx}(0, t) in the kalimba page’s convention, and its bending moment, a turning push, F_2 = EI\,u_{xx}(0, t); here E is steel’s Young’s modulus and I the second moment of area (derived on the kalimba page).
Clarinet and flute. The open end is a small source whose strength is the rate at which the outflow changes, and the pressure slope -u_x(L, t) sets that rate. At a distance R in open air, p(t) = -(S/4\pi R)\,u_x(L, t - R/c_0), where S is the area of the opening and c_0 the speed of sound. For most notes the “open end” is the first open tone holes, and the bell radiates the lowest notes and the high partials above the tone holes’ cutoff; a flute also radiates from its embouchure hole (Fletcher and Rossing, above, chapters 7, 8, 15 and 16).

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
The same recipe
For a plucked or struck note, the last link of the chain is the only one that creates frequencies: the motion obeys u_{tt} = -Au, with the object’s boundary conditions and its start or drive. Here the operator A turns a shape into minus the acceleration it causes. For the instruments left to ring, every motion is a sum of the object’s own shapes, the eigenfunctions X_n with AX_n = \lambda_nX_n, each swinging at f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi. The kettledrum is the exception: it radiates into the unbounded air, which takes it outside this argument (fold), so its ratios here are measured.6
6 A kettledrum measured by A. H. Benade, Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics, Oxford University Press, 1976, chapter 9, pp. 143–144, as tabulated by HyperPhysics, The Timpani, Georgia State University: spoke modes at about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times the lowest.


PreciselyThe theorem, and its three names uses Hilbert spaces

What carries over from the string: on a bounded object with a reasonable edge, each of these operators is self-adjoint and \geq 0 and has a compact resolvent, so it has an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions, and drifts split off. The three routes are Sturm–Liouville theory for strings and tubes, a compact Green’s operator for bars, and Rellich’s theorem for drums (R. Courant and D. Hilbert, Methods of Mathematical Physics, vol. 1, Interscience, 1953, chapters III (symmetric kernels), V and VI; L. C. Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2010, sections 5.7 and 6.5.1). The kettledrum’s radiation, sound carried away into the unbounded air, makes its problem non-self-adjoint, and its full air loading is beyond this page; the air’s added mass alone would keep it inside the theorem, as the drum page’s toy model of the air does.
A Sturm–Liouville problem is -(p\,X')' + q\,X = \lambda\,w\,X on a bounded interval, with p, w > 0 and one condition at each end of the form \alpha X + \beta X' = 0; the string (p = c^2, q = 0, w = 1) and the tubes, open or closed at each end, are of this form, and its eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis (R. Courant and D. Hilbert, Methods of Mathematical Physics, vol. 1, Interscience, 1953, chapters V and VI). For a bar, (A + 1)^{-1} is an integral operator with a kernel continuous on [0, L]^2, the Green’s operator, which is compact and self-adjoint, so the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators applies to it, and its eigenfunctions are A’s. For a drumhead, Rellich’s theorem says that on a bounded region, every sequence of shapes that vanish on the rim and have \iint u^2 and \iint |\nabla u|^2 bounded has a subsequence converging in mean square; this makes (A + 1)^{-1} compact (L. C. Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2010, section 5.7). A drift occurs only when A has the eigenvalue 0: on this page, for the glockenspiel bar.


In short, 
c_n = |H(f_n)|\,w_n\,|a_n| ,
 with w_n the route weight (for one input; on the kalimba, mode n’s shear V_n and moment M_n at the clamp combine as {|H_1V_n + H_2M_n|}, and a small drum’s points act as one): the pitch traces back to the spectrum of A, the timbre to the start, the route, H and the spacing of that spectrum, and the duration to the losses.

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A piano
A piano note is clear, but its upper partials run slightly sharp of the whole-number lines because the steel wire resists bending as well as being pulled straight.7 So an exact 2 : 1 octave beats, and tuners widen octaves.8
7 N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 12 (the piano); Wikipedia, Inharmonicity.8 O. L. Railsback, “Scale temperament as applied to piano tuning”, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 9 (1938), 274 (DOI); Wikipedia, Piano acoustics.
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  Middle C, struck an eighth of the way along (books commonly give 1/7 to 1/9, though on modern pianos many notes are struck nearer the end: Conklin), where the 8th mode stands still, so in the model its stem is zero. Computed: the stem positions, with B = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴, a rough value for a middle C wire. Modelled: each mode starts in proportion to its height under the hammer, with a roll-off for the felt. Illustrative: the fading times.

The spectrum is f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, where f_0 is the lowest frequency the wire would have without stiffness and the small number B measures the stiffness.

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A kalimba
A kalimba tine gives a click, then a clean note: its first overtone, far off the lines and strong at the attack, dies within a fraction of a second.9
9 D. M. F. Chapman, The sound of the African thumb piano (kalimba), Acoustics’08 Paris, paper 5aMUf1, Acoustical Society of America, 2008: one dominant overtone, at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, dying away quickly after the attack.
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  A tine at A4, 440 Hz, pushed at its tip and let go. Computed: the stem positions and each stem's starting height, the push on the bridge (the shear force at the clamp) from the smooth bent start (a cubic, derived on the kalimba page). Illustrative: the fading times, chosen to match Chapman's observation that the overtones die within a fraction of a second; the stems shrink as each partial fades. The tine is drawn as it moves; in displacement its first overtone is only 2.5% of the fundamental, so the picture shows mostly the first mode, while in the push on the bridge it starts at 55%.

The spectrum is in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55, and f_1 \propto 1/L^2, where L is the tine’s free length: half the length sounds two octaves up.10 So makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge.11
10 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 2 (strings and bars).11 Kalimba Magic, on tuning tines.Deep dive: the kalimba →

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A glockenspiel
A glockenspiel gives a bright, clear note although its overtones sit off the lines: they are high and die quickly, leaving the fundamental.12 Its bar is the kalimba tine’s kind of steel bar with both ends free, resting on soft supports and struck with a mallet: 
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \ \text{ at } x = 0 \text{ and } x = L, \\
u(x, 0) = 0, \qquad u_t(x, 0) = v_0(x).
\end{gathered}
 Here u(x, t) is the bar’s displacement, L its length, \kappa^2 its stiffness over its mass, and v_0 the mallet’s blow (fold).
12 G. P. Scavone, Percussion instruments, course notes, CCRMA, Stanford University, 1999: “All but the lowest transverse mode die out quickly when the bar is struck”; Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 19 (mallet percussion).13 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapters 2 and 19.Writing \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, the eigenvalues solve \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1, which puts the frequencies in the ratios 1 : 2.756 : 5.404, off the lines.13 Two eigenvalues are 0: the bar sliding or tilting without bending, drifts that move as a + bt, for constants a and b, and make no sound.

  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  A bar tuned to C6, 1047 Hz, struck a little off its middle. Computed: the stem positions. Illustrative: the starting strengths and the fading times. The bar is drawn on its two supports, at its fundamental's still points.




DetailsWhere the equation comes from

Here \kappa^2 = EI/\rho S: E is steel’s Young’s modulus, I the second moment of area of the cross-section, \rho the density and S the cross-section’s area; v_0 is the mallet’s blow, concentrated where it lands. The equation is the kalimba tine’s beam equation, from the same slice of bar (derived on the kalimba page). Only the ends differ: on soft supports both ends are free, so at each end no bending moment and no shear force act, u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0. The supports are taken as not holding the bar at all; resting at the fundamental’s still points, they are where that mode does not move.





PreciselyThe spectrum, step by step uses a 2×2 determinant

With \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, X = b_1\cos\beta x + b_2\sin\beta x + b_3\cosh\beta x + b_4\sinh\beta x. The free left end, X''(0) = X'''(0) = 0, gives b_3 = b_1 and b_4 = b_2. With c_1 = \cos\beta L, s_1 = \sin\beta L, c_2 = \cosh\beta L and s_2 = \sinh\beta L (hyperbolic functions), the free right end gives (c_2 - c_1)b_1 + (s_2 - s_1)b_2 = 0 and (s_2 + s_1)b_1 + (c_2 - c_1)b_2 = 0, whose determinant is (c_2 - c_1)^2 - (s_2^2 - s_1^2) = 2 - 2c_1c_2. So \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1, with roots \beta L = 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, \dots For \lambda = 0, X'''' = 0 with free ends leaves exactly X = a + bx: two eigenfunctions with eigenvalue 0, whose coordinates move as q = a + bt. The fundamental’s still points, where X_1 = 0, are at 0.224L and 0.776L (computed).

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
Drums
A bass drum booms with no clear pitch; a kettledrum, one of the timpani, plays a note. Both heads are a stretched skin whose ideal frequencies fall between the lines.14 On the kettledrum the air pulls the spoke modes, with still lines through the center and no still circle inside the rim, near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base, and the round modes, with no line through the center, radiate away within a fraction of a second.15 Step through it:

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A violin, bowed
A bowed string holds a steady note with its partials exactly on the lines: the bow’s friction grabs the string and lets it slip once per period, so the string repeats one cycle, as Helmholtz saw through a vibration microscope in 1860.16
16 H. Helmholtz, “On the motion of the strings of a violin”, Proceedings of the Philosophical Society of Glasgow 5 (1860–64), 17–21, read 19 December 1860 (archive.org).
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  Helmholtz motion of an open G string, 196 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, computed for the ideal string, with strength 1/n, without the wooden body. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the string's modes, on every line too. The picture is the sum of the first 40 modes; dashed, the corner's path, two arcs of a parabola.
