title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A flute
A flute plays a steady note on the lines. It is a tube of air open at both ends,17 kept going by a jet blown across the embouchure hole.18 An open end holds room pressure, so the tube’s own spectrum is the string’s, f_n = nc/2L, with c the speed of sound and L the tube’s length: on the lines too.19 It overblows to the octave with a faster, narrower airstream.20
17 J. Wolfe, Flute acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: open at both ends.18 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 16 (flutes); Wolfe, Flute acoustics: the jet.19 J. Wolfe, Pipes and harmonics, UNSW: open and closed ends; Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 8 (pipes).20 Wolfe, Flute acoustics: registers.
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  A steady D4, 294 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, all on the lines; their strengths, 1/n², are an illustrative choice. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the open tube's modes, on every line too. Picture: the air in the tube, darker where the pressure is higher, with thin slabs of air that bunch where it is squeezed.

Deep dive: the flute, on the clarinet page →

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A clarinet
A clarinet sounds a hollow note nearly an octave below a flute of the same length. Its tube is closed at the reed, so its spectrum is f_n = (2n - 1)c/4L: the odd multiples of c/4L, half the flute’s lowest frequency.21 So in the low register the odd partials are strong and the even ones weak.22
21 Wolfe, Pipes and harmonics: a pipe closed at one end.22 J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW: a clarinet about an octave below a flute of the same length; J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: strong odd harmonics in the low register.
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  A steady D3, 147 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, on every line, strong odd and faint even ones; the exact strengths are an illustrative choice after Wolfe's description. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the tube's modes, on the odd lines only. Picture: the air column, closed at the reed on the left, drawn with the odd partials only; the faint even ones are left out of the picture.

Deep dive: the clarinet →

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A harmonica
A harmonica reed’s own overtones sit far off the lines, yet its note has partials only on the lines, odd and even both strong. You hear the air, not the reed: the reed lets one identical puff through its slot per cycle, and repeating puffs have only whole-number partials.23
23 C. Pykett, The physics of free reeds, 2023: the sound comes from the puffs; odd and even harmonics.
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  A C5 reed, 523 Hz, blown. Stems: the sound's partials, at whole-number multiples of the playing frequency, computed from the puff drawn on the right: one puff per cycle, open for about 30% of it, a shape chosen for illustration. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the reed's modes, at 1 and 6.27 times its lowest; the playing frequency sits somewhat below the lowest, drawn here at 1. The reed is drawn in its first mode, and the slot is drawn open only while the tip is above the plate.

Deep dive: the harmonica →

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A theremin
A theremin’s tone glides as the hand moves, without the instrument being touched.24 It comes from coil-and-capacitor circuits, LC circuits, whose charge swings like a mass on a spring: 
\ddot q = -\frac{1}{LC}\,q .
 Here q is the charge, \ddot q its second time derivative, L the coil’s inductance and C the capacitance (fold). An amplifier keeps the swing at a steady size.25
24 Wikipedia, Theremin.25 Wikipedia, Electronic oscillator: an amplifier feeding a tuned circuit in phase, its amplitude limited by a nonlinearity.26 Wikipedia, Theremin: two radio-frequency oscillators below 500 kHz.The spectrum is one frequency, f = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}), a radio frequency below 500 kHz.26 The instrument runs two such circuits, one changed by the hand, and outputs the difference of their frequencies, which is audible (heterodyning).

  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  An idealized sine theremin at A4, 440 Hz: one stem. A real theremin's tone is not a pure sine: it has overtones. No resonator ticks: the circuits' own frequencies are radio frequencies, far beyond this ruler, and the tone you hear is the difference of two of them. Picture: one coil-and-capacitor circuit, its charge sloshing between the plates, slowed to about one swing a second.




DetailsWhere the equation comes from

Here q is the charge on the capacitor, L the coil’s inductance and C the capacitance, so the operator is A = 1/LC, one number. Kirchhoff’s voltage law, which balances voltages as Newton’s law balances forces, says that the voltages around a closed loop add to zero. A capacitor holding charge q has the voltage q/C across it; a coil carrying the current I = \dot q has the voltage L\,\dot I. Around the loop, L\,\ddot q + q/C = 0, that is, \ddot q = -q/LC: the coil plays the mass and 1/C the spring’s stiffness. For ideal parts both laws are linear, so no small-motion step is needed.





DetailsHow two radio frequencies make one audible tone

A mixer multiplies the two oscillators’ signals, and \sin(2\pi f_1t)\sin(2\pi f_2t) = \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 - f_2)t) - \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 + f_2)t); a filter keeps the difference. With both near a few hundred kilohertz, a hand that changes one circuit’s capacitance by a small fraction moves the difference across the whole audible range. Real theremins’ mixers and circuits add overtones, on the whole-number lines of the difference frequency, since the output repeats at that rate.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Violin · Kalimba → · Glossary
The ends. A flute is open at both ends; a clarinet is closed at the reed. A tube closed at one end fits a quarter of a wave where an open tube fits a half, so the same length sounds an octave lower and has modes only at the odd multiples of its lowest frequency. Hold the blow button on the clarinet, then switch the same tube to a flute and blow again. In the demo, the register key stands in for overblowing (on a flute, a faster, narrower airstream).
What you hear works as in post 1: the frequencies give the pitch, and their sizes the loudness and timbre. The room keeps those frequencies (post 2).

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
How the sound gets out
The sound leaves through the open holes and the bell. For most notes much of it leaves through the first open tone hole, the tube’s effective open end; the bell radiates the lowest notes, and the high partials, which pass the open holes as if they were closed.1 A flute also radiates from its embouchure hole, one of its two open ends. At an open end of area S, at distance x = L from the reed, the slope p_x of the tube’s pressure p(x, t), above room pressure, pushes air in and out, and that pulsing flow is what the room hears: at a distance R in open air, with c the speed of sound, the sound is 
p_{\text{out}}(t) = -\frac{S}{4\pi R}\,p_x\Big(L,\ t - \frac{R}{c}\Big).
 The slope keeps every frequency and weights each frequency f by its wavenumber 2\pi f/c.
1 J. Wolfe, Cutoff frequencies, crossfingering and half-holing in woodwinds, UNSW: below the cutoff much of the power leaves through the first open tone hole; “Above fc, a large fraction of the output sound is radiated from the bell.” See also Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 15.


DetailsWhere the formula for the sound comes from derivatives

Let v(t) be the outward speed of the air at the open end. With \rho the air’s density, Newton’s law on the last thin slab of air is \rho\,v_t = -p_x(L, t), so the volume of air flowing out each second, U = Sv, changes at the rate U_t = -(S/\rho)\,p_x(L, t). An opening much smaller than the wavelength acts as a simple source, a small pulsating sphere, whose sound at a distance R is \rho\,U_t(t - R/c)/4\pi R: it arrives R/c seconds later and falls off as 1/R (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapters 7 and 8). Together these give the formula above. This is for one small opening radiating freely in all directions; with several open holes and the bell, the sound is a sum of such terms, one per opening.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
The tube’s equation
The frequencies come from the air column’s own shapes. For the pressure p(x, t) in a tube of length L, Newton’s law on a thin slab of air gives the string’s wave equation again, now for the pressure (the flute’s entry derives it): 
\begin{gathered}
p_{tt} = -Ap, \qquad Ap = -c^2p_{xx}, \\
c^2 = \frac{K}{\rho} .
\end{gathered}
 Here K is the air’s bulk modulus, its resistance to being squeezed, \rho its density, and c the speed of sound.
The ends are part of the operator A, and they are all that differ:

An open end meets the room, so the pressure there is room pressure, p = 0, a Dirichlet condition.2 The flute has two: p(0) = p(L) = 0.
The clarinet’s reed is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move, and air that never moves feels no net push: the pressure has no slope, p_x(0) = 0, a Neumann condition. Its bell is open, p(L) = 0.

2 J. Wolfe, Pipes and harmonics, UNSW: at an open end the “sound pressure (difference from atmospheric) is close to zero”.


DetailsThe reed end, the end correction, and what the model leaves out

Let \xi(x, t) be how far the air that normally sits at x has moved along the tube. Newton’s law on a slab is \rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x. At the reed the air cannot move, so \xi = 0 there at all times, so \xi_{tt} = 0, and Newton’s law gives p_x = 0. The air just outside an open end moves with the air inside, so the tube acts slightly longer, by about 0.6 of its radius, an amount called the end correction (J. Wolfe, Pipes and harmonics, UNSW: “usually about 0.6 times the radius”). The model assumes a narrow cylindrical tube, small pressure changes and no friction at the walls. A real clarinet’s bore is not exactly cylindrical, and its holes and bell matter; they refine the numbers, not the picture (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapters 8 and 15). So a real clarinet sounds a bit less than an octave below a flute: the two differ a little in length, and the mouthpiece, the bell and the open ends change the effective length (J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW: “There are complications due to end corrections”).

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
Two tubes, two spectra
The shapes the operator only stretches, AX_n = \lambda_nX_n, swing at f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi. With the flute’s ends they are the string’s sines; with the clarinet’s they are cosines that fit an odd number of quarter waves: 
\begin{aligned}
&\text{flute:} && X_n = \sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}, \\
& && f_n = n\,\frac{c}{2L}, \\
&\text{clarinet:} && X_n = \cos\frac{(2n - 1)\pi x}{2L}, \\
& && f_n = (2n - 1)\,\frac{c}{4L} .
\end{aligned}
 The flute’s modes sit at 1, 2, 3, 4, … times its lowest frequency, the clarinet’s at 1, 3, 5, 7, … times its lowest,3 and the clarinet’s lowest, c/4L, is half the flute’s, c/2L: an octave lower for the same length.4 Blown, the tube is a self-sustained oscillation (appendix): this step decides which notes can sound; the drive fixes the exact frequencies, at multiples of the playing frequency f_p.
3 J. Wolfe, Pipes and harmonics, UNSW: closed cylindrical bores “have only odd harmonics starting one octave lower”.4 J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW: for the same length, the closed pipe’s lowest frequency “c/4L = 140 Hz – one octave lower than the flute”.


PreciselyThe two spectra, step by step derivatives

Writing \lambda = c^2k^2, the mode equation -c^2X'' = \lambda X becomes X'' = -k^2X, solved by X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx, with f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi = ck/2\pi.
Flute. X(0) = 0 forces a = 0, and X(L) = 0 needs \sin kL = 0, so kL = n\pi: one half wave, two half waves, and so on. So \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2 and f_n = nc/2L.
Clarinet. X'(0) = bk = 0 forces b = 0, leaving X = \cos kx, and X(L) = 0 needs \cos kL = 0, so kL = (2n - 1)\pi/2: one quarter wave, three quarter waves, and so on. So \lambda_n = \big((2n - 1)\pi c/2L\big)^2 and f_n = (2n - 1)c/4L.
As for the string, integration by parts rules out \lambda \le 0, and every pressure shape is a sum of these modes; the appendix says when such a sum is guaranteed.




  
  
  The tubes' modes, as multiples of each tube's lowest frequency: open at both ends (top), every line; closed at one end (bottom), the odd lines only. The stems mark where modes can sit; their heights carry no meaning here.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
The chain in one line
Put together, partial n of the blown note reaches your ear with the size 
c_n = |H(nf_p)| \cdot |P_n| ,
 where f_p is the playing frequency, P_n partial n of the pressure slope p_x(L, t) at the open end, and H the factor of the openings and the room. Pitch traces back to the playing frequency; timbre to the modes, the breath and the openings; loudness to the breath; duration to the player.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
Blown: one repeating cycle
A blown tube settles into one motion that repeats, close to one of its modes. The clarinet’s reed acts as a valve that the pressure in the mouthpiece opens and closes, so the air column drives the reed that feeds it.5 On a flute, a jet of air blown across the embouchure hole does the reed’s job.6 The oscillation runs near one of the tube’s modes, usually the lowest, with L the tube up to the first open hole: the fingers choose the note by choosing L.
5 J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: “the reed acts like an oscillating valve”.6 J. Wolfe, Flute acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: “The flutist blows a rapid jet of air across the embouchure hole”; “The flute is open at both ends.”7 J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: “the sound spectrum in the low register has strong first and third harmonics, but weak second and fourth”.8 J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: added harmonics make the sound brighter and louder; soft playing in the linear range gives “few high harmonics”.The tube’s modes pick the strong partials. The tube’s modes are odd multiples only, but its sound may have even ones too: in the low register the second and fourth harmonics are weak, since no mode of the tube supports them, and the first and third strong.7 The breath sets the loudness and the brightness: blowing harder adds high harmonics.8


  
  
  The blown sounds, as multiples of the note being played: the flute (top) has every whole-number multiple; the clarinet (bottom) has strong odd multiples and faint even ones. The demos' sounds are made this way; the exact strengths are an illustrative choice.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
section: Overblowing: a twelfth or an octave
text:
Overblowing: a twelfth or an octave
The clarinet has no mode at twice its lowest frequency, so it overblows to three times. When a clarinetist presses the register key, the tube jumps to its next mode, 3\times its lowest frequency: an octave and a fifth, called a twelfth.9 A flutist overblows with a faster jet, and the flute’s next mode is 2\times its lowest, an octave.10
9 J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW: “the second register of the clarinet is a musical twelfth above the first”.10 J. Wolfe, Flute acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: blowing harder or narrowing the lips gives “a faster jet”, and the flute “jumps up” to the octave, 2f_1.


DetailsHow the register key picks out the 3× mode

The register key opens a small hole, which for one low note lies a third of the way from the reed to the first open hole. An open hole pulls the pressure there toward room pressure, which spoils the fundamental, a mode that needs pressure variation at that point. For one note in the low register the hole sits right where that note’s 3f_1 mode has no pressure variation anyway, so the open hole does not disturb that mode. For the other notes the hole is off that point, and a second effect helps: the air in a small hole has mass, so the faster it must move back and forth, the harder it is to move. At the fundamental’s lower frequency the hole leaks enough to spoil that mode; at the 3f_1 mode’s higher frequency it acts almost as a plug: “high frequency waves pass by as though it were closed”. Either way the tube jumps to the 3f_1 mode. (J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW)

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Piano · Beyond · When does an equation have a spectrum? → · Glossary
A drumhead’s frequencies fall between the whole-number lines, so a plain drum thuds. A kettledrum plays a note because the air its head drags along pulls one set of modes close to 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, and the way it is struck and the way its modes fade leave mostly those. Tap the head anywhere, then tap dead center and compare.
What you hear works as in post 1: the frequencies give the pitch, their sizes the loudness and timbre, and their fading the duration. The room keeps those frequencies (post 2).

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
The whole skin sounds
The sound leaves from the whole skin, and the round modes radiate best. Every point of the head pushes the air with its acceleration u_{tt}, where u(x, y, t) is the head’s height at the point (x, y), and your ear hears the sum of the pushes, which keeps every frequency. When the drum is small compared with the wavelength, they reach your ear almost together, so a mode X sounds in proportion to the net volume it pushes, |\iint X\,dA|. That is zero for every mode with a still line through the center (below). So the round modes, those with no line through the center, pump air like a piston and lose their energy within a fraction of a second, while such a mode pushes the air up on one side as it pulls it down on the other, radiates weakly, and rings longer.1
1 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 18 (drums).

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
The head’s shapes
A round head’s shapes are built from Bessel functions, whose zeros are not whole-number multiples of the first. A head with tension T per unit length and mass \sigma per unit area obeys u_{tt} = -Au with 
A = -c^2\,\Delta, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\sigma}, \qquad \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy},
 acting on shapes that are zero on the rim.
On a round drum of radius a, the modes, the shapes A only stretches (-\Delta X = k^2X, X = 0 on the rim, \lambda = c^2k^2), separate into a function of the distance r from the center times a function of the angle \theta (separation of variables).

Around the center, the shape must come back to itself after a turn, which allows only \cos m\theta and \sin m\theta with m a whole number: m straight still lines through the center, like spokes.
Outward from the center, the shape is a Bessel function J_m(kr), which plays the sine’s part: it wiggles like a cosine whose swings slowly shrink.

The rim requires J_m(ka) = 0. Writing j_{m,n} for the n-th positive zero of J_m, 
\begin{gathered}
X_{m,n} = J_m\!\Big(\frac{j_{m,n}\,r}{a}\Big)\cos m\theta \ \text{ and } \\ J_m\!\Big(\frac{j_{m,n}\,r}{a}\Big)\sin m\theta, \\
\lambda_{m,n} = \frac{c^2j_{m,n}^2}{a^2}, \qquad f_{m,n} = \frac{c\,j_{m,n}}{2\pi a} .
\end{gathered}
 Relative to the lowest, the frequencies are 1, 1.593, 2.136, 2.295, …, between the lines.2 For a struck note this is the only step that creates frequencies.
2 Wikipedia, Vibrations of a circular membrane.










J₀ (starts at 1)J₁ (starts at 0)
2.4055.5208.654
r →

Why the zeros miss the lines. The zeros of J_0, 2.405, 5.520, 8.654, …, come at nearly even steps of about \pi, but the first is short, about 0.77\pi, so the later ones are not multiples of it: 1 : 2.30 : 3.60.



DetailsSeparating the mode equation in polar coordinates the chain rule

In the coordinates r and \theta the Laplacian reads \Delta X = X_{rr} + X_r/r + X_{\theta\theta}/r^2, a standard change of variables quoted here (Wikipedia, Laplace operator in two dimensions). Substituting X = R(r)\,\Theta(\theta) into -\Delta X = k^2X and multiplying by r^2/R\Theta gives 
\frac{r^2R'' + rR' + k^2r^2R}{R} = -\frac{\Theta''}{\Theta} .
 The left side depends only on r and the right only on \theta, so both equal one constant. Going once around must bring \Theta back to itself, so -\Theta'' = m^2\Theta with m a whole number: the eigenvalue problem of a loop of string (appendix). What remains is Bessel’s equation, r^2R'' + rR' + (k^2r^2 - m^2)R = 0. It depends on r only through kr. Of its two independent solutions, J_m(kr) is finite at the center; the other becomes infinite there, which would take infinite energy (Wikipedia, Bessel function).





PreciselyWhy these are all the modes, and why the pairs are exact

These are all the modes: expanding any mode in a Fourier series in \theta reduces -\Delta X = k^2X, term by term, to Bessel’s equation for each m. Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to exactly two modes because Bessel functions of different whole-number orders never share a positive zero, Bourget’s conjecture, proved by Siegel in 1929 (C. L. Siegel, “Über einige Anwendungen diophantischer Approximationen”, Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, Physikalisch-mathematische Klasse, 1929, no. 1; English translation in On Some Applications of Diophantine Approximations, Edizioni della Normale, 2014). The round head’s symmetry shows up as this multiplicity of 2. For large n the zeros approach j_{m,n} \approx (n + \tfrac m2 - \tfrac14)\pi: evenly spaced for one m, shifted by an amount that depends on m. This page computes them numerically.


In the panel, each stem is one j_{m,n}/j_{0,1}, its height how strongly that mode sounds at one point of the head, not in the net volume, after your last strike; tap a stem to see and hear it.


    Partials of the last strike · tap a stem

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
Where the equation comes from
The sheet around a small patch pulls along the patch’s whole edge, and for small slopes the upward parts of those pulls add up, by the divergence theorem, to T\,\Delta u per unit area. Newton’s law gives3 
\sigma\,u_{tt} = T\,\Delta u .
 The Laplacian \Delta u measures how far a point sits below the average height of the points around it, so tension pulls each point toward that average.
3 N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 3 (membranes).


DetailsThe patch, step by step the divergence theorem

A small patch D has mass \iint_D\sigma\,dA. A drumhead is a membrane: a sheet with no stiffness of its own, stretched with the same tension in every direction, so across each short piece ds of the patch’s edge the sheet outside pulls with the force T\,ds, along the surface and outward. For small slopes the upward part of that pull is T\,\partial_nu\,ds, with \partial_nu the slope outward across the edge. Adding these around the edge, the divergence theorem gives 
T\oint_{\partial D}\partial_nu\,ds = T\iint_D\Delta u\,dA .
 So \iint_D \sigma\,u_{tt}\,dA = T\iint_D\Delta u\,dA for every patch, however small, and the integrands agree at every point. In one dimension the same step is u_x(b) - u_x(a) = \int_a^b u_{xx}\,dx, the string’s. The model assumes small slopes and a uniform tension, and leaves out bending stiffness, damping and the air on both sides of the head; the air comes back for the kettledrum.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
Where you strike
A sharp strike starts each mode in proportion to how far that mode moves at the point struck. Every mode with spokes stands still at the center, so a strike at dead center sounds only the round modes.



DetailsHow strongly a strike starts each mode, in this model integrals over an area

A brief push at a point p gives mode X_i a starting speed in proportion to X_i(p). We model what you hear as the speed of the head at a listening point q, which picks up mode i in proportion to X_i(q); dividing by \iint X_i^2\,dA removes the arbitrary size of each shape. So mode i sounds with weight X_i(p)\,X_i(q)\big/\iint X_i^2\,dA. A real drum’s sound comes from its whole head, which favours the round modes (see above); this model ignores that.


Sand shows a mode’s still lines, as Ernst Chladni showed on metal plates in the 1780s.4
4 Wikipedia, Ernst Chladni.

  
  
  Sprinkle fresh sandHear this note
  
  Each button drives the drumhead at one of its own frequencies, given as a multiple of the lowest. Every grain is jostled in proportion to how much the head moves under it, so grains drift until they reach a place where the head stays still. Chladni used stiff metal plates, whose operator involves bending, not tension; the sand behaves the same way on both.





DetailsWhere the sand collects, and the history polar coordinates

The mode J_m(kr)\cos m\theta with k = j_{m,n}/a is zero where \cos m\theta = 0, at 2m angles that pair up into m lines through the center, and on the n - 1 circles inside the rim where J_m(kr) = 0. Those are the lines where the sand collects.
In 1808 Chladni showed his sand patterns on plates, bowed along their edges, to the French Institute in Paris, and Napoleon offered a prize for explaining them. Sophie Germain won it in 1816, the first woman to receive the Paris Academy’s grand prize in mathematics, with a theory that was still incomplete (P. Lynch, “The ‘extraordinary talent and superior genius’ of Sophie Germain”, The Irish Times, January 2020, also on That’s Maths). Gustav Kirchhoff gave the full theory of vibrating plates, with the correct edge conditions, in 1850 (G. Kirchhoff, “Über das Gleichgewicht und die Bewegung einer elastischen Scheibe”, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 40, 1850, 51–88). Finding the still lines and finding the frequencies are one problem, with the plate’s own operator in place of the drumhead’s.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
The chain in one line
To leading (monopole) order, for a drum small compared with the wavelength, a mode X of frequency f, started by the strike with the amount s, reaches your ear with the size 
c = |H(f)| \cdot (2\pi f)^2\,\Big|\iint X\,dA\Big| \cdot |s| ,
 where H is the room’s factor. Modes with a still line through the center get nothing at this order; they radiate at the next, as push–pull pairs (a dipole for one line, weaker for more), weaker but long-ringing: on a kettledrum they are the note. A kettledrum is only borderline small (2\pi af/v \approx 0.8 near 130 Hz, v the speed of sound in air), and its bowl blocks the underside. Pitch traces back to the spectrum of A; timbre to the strike, the net-volume weight, H and the spacing; loudness to the strike; duration to the losses.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
One drumhead, two drums

  Each picture is one mode seen from above, labelled (m, n): m still lines through the center, n still circles counting the rim. Dark and light patches move in opposite directions. The ring gives its kind:

  Each stem is one mode: its position is its frequency as a multiple of a base an octave below the (1,1) mode, so the (1,1) sits at 2×, and its height is how strongly the strike starts it; dashed stems are modes that have faded. Stems on the dashed whole-number lines make a note. Each drum plays at its own size: the bass drum's lowest mode near 50 Hz, the timpani's (1,1) at 131 Hz (C3). Measured ratios puts the kettledrum's spoke modes on 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 times the base, the pattern a kettledrum measured by A. H. Benade (Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics, 1976, chapter 9) sits close to: about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times its lowest mode, as tabulated by HyperPhysics. This toy model gets only halfway there; the fold below gives its numbers and what it misses.





DetailsThe toy model, the kettle, and other drums integrals over an area

Where each drum is struck. A concert bass drum is played slightly off center; center playing, punchier and with less sustain, is kept for rhythmic passages (A. Graham, “Proper Playing Areas”, The Instrumentalist, September 2017; “How to play the bass drum properly”, with Keith Aleo, Interlochen Center for the Arts, 3 April 2023). There the spoke modes move little, so among the lowest modes the round ones dominate. For the timpani’s strike, halfway to three-quarters of the way out (below), with the weight |X(p)|\big/\big(\iint X^2\,dA\big)^{1/2} for a strike at p on a head of radius 1, the lowest round mode (0,1) has 1.09 at the center, 0.73 at halfway and 0.37 at three-quarters, while the spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) have between 0.74 and 1.19 anywhere from halfway to three-quarters. Nearer halfway the stick also sits close to the inner still circles of the modes (0,2), (1,2), (2,2) and (3,2), which lie between 0.44 and 0.65 of the radius, which quiets those too. The clear note also relies on the remaining modes being weaker or fading faster, which this page takes from measurements rather than deriving (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 18).
The air’s mass. Treat the air on both sides of the head as not squeezable, and each mode, locally, as a ripple of wavenumber k = j_{m,n}/a, whose crests are about \pi/k apart. The air such a ripple sets moving reaches about 1/k from the head on each side, which adds a mass of about 2\rho/k per unit area (\rho \approx 1.2 kg/m³ for air) to the head’s own \sigma: 
\begin{gathered}
\omega^2 = \frac{T k^2}{\sigma + 2\rho/k}, \\
f \propto \frac{k}{\sqrt{\sigma + 2\rho/k}} ,
\end{gathered}
 so coarse shapes, with small k, slow down most. This is added mass: it can only lower frequencies. A typical Mylar kettledrum head has \sigma \approx 0.26 kg/m², on drums of radius 0.32 and 0.355 m (T. A. Packer, Acoustics of the Orchestral Kettledrum, master’s thesis, University of Durham, 1993, appendix B); with a = 0.33 m, 2\rho a/\sigma \approx 3.0. The spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) move from 1 : 1.34 : 1.67 : 1.98 to 1 : 1.42 : 1.83 : 2.24, halfway to 1.5 : 2 : 2.5. The rest of the shift comes from a full calculation of the air inside and around a finite head (R. S. Christian, R. E. Davis, A. Tubis, C. A. Anderson, R. I. Mills and T. D. Rossing, “Effects of air loading on timpani membrane vibrations”, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 76, 1984, 1336–1345), not from the kettle’s air spring, its uniform pressure.
The kettle. The nearly sealed kettle (it has a small vent) acts as a spring on the volume the head sweeps, V = \iint u\,dA, adding \tfrac12\eta V^2 to the stored energy for some constant \eta > 0. The operator gains the term (\eta/\sigma)\,\mathbf 1\langle\mathbf 1, \cdot\rangle, where \mathbf 1 is the constant shape: a term of rank one. Every mode with m \ge 1 has \iint X\,dA = 0, because \int_0^{2\pi}\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0, so it keeps its frequency exactly. Only the round modes are raised, and since the new term couples them to each other, their shapes change too; the step-through treats each on its own. In general, added stiffness never lowers a frequency and added mass never raises one, by the min–max principle.
The bass drum’s second head. A bass drum has a head on each end of its shell, coupled through the air inside, which splits its two lowest modes, (0,1) and (1,1); “it is common practice to tune the lowest modes of the two heads about a musical fourth apart” (HyperPhysics, The Bass Drum). Not modelled here.
Other drums. The tabla and the mridangam reach near-whole-number overtones a different way: a patch of paste loads the center of the head, which makes its density non-uniform, outside this page’s model (C. V. Raman and S. Kumar, “Musical drums with harmonic overtones”, Nature 104, 1920, 500; C. V. Raman, “The Indian musical drums”, Proceedings of the Indian Academy of Sciences A 1, 1934, 179–188).

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
Two drums, heard
A bass drum booms with no clear pitch. Struck slightly off center, it starts mostly round modes; players muffle the head with a leg or a towel for short notes.5
5 A. Graham, “Proper Playing Areas”, The Instrumentalist, September 2017; “How to play the bass drum properly”, with Keith Aleo, Interlochen Center for the Arts, 3 April 2023.6 HyperPhysics, The Timpani, tabulating A. H. Benade’s measurements (Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics, 1976, chapter 9, pp. 143–144): modes at 1.504, 2.00, 2.494 and 2.979 times the lowest. Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 18, on the air loading.7 HyperPhysics, The Timpani: “The head is struck about halfway to three quarters of the way out from the center.”8 Institute of Musical Acoustics (Wiener Klangstil), University of Music and Performing Arts Vienna, The Viennese timpani: “Der Grundton (Mode 11) …, die Quinte (Mode 21) … und die Oktave (Mode 31)”.A kettledrum plays a note. The air the head drags along moves the spoke modes, those with lines through the center and no still circle inside the rim, near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base;6 the stick, about halfway to three-quarters of the way out, starts the lowest round mode weakly;7 and the round modes die fast. What is left nearly repeats: a note, whose principal tone is the (1,1) mode, with the (2,1) a fifth and the (3,1) an octave above it.8



PreciselyWhich octave the ear names

The modes above the (1,1) sit a fifth, an octave and a major tenth (ratio 5 : 2) above it. The pitch rule of post 1 would put the pitch an octave lower, at the base, and HyperPhysics notes that “the missing fundamental effect might then give you the pitch C2” for a drum tuned to C3 (HyperPhysics, The Timpani). Which octave the ear names is one of the exceptions post 1 lists, and this series doesn’t settle it.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
Next
Turn the question around: if you could hear every frequency a drum makes, could you work out its shape? Can you hear the shape of a drum?

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← The gallery · Clarinet → · Glossary
A light touch is a damper at one point. It drains every shape of the string that moves under the finger and spares the shapes that stand still there. At the middle, the spared shapes are exactly the shapes of a note an octave up; no frequency moves. String players call these touched notes harmonics.1 Pluck the string, then pick a point to touch and pluck again.
What you hear works as in post 1: the frequencies give the pitch, their sizes the loudness and timbre, and their fading the duration. Once the body’s own ring at the start has died away, the body and the room keep those frequencies (post 2).

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
section: How the sound reaches the air
text:
How the sound reaches the air
The sound reaches the air through the bridge. The string is too thin to push the air itself, so it pushes the bridge, a carved maple piece standing on the top plate and held there by the strings’ pressure,2 with the force F(t) = -T\,u_x(L, t), where u(x, t) is the string’s height at time t and distance x from the nut near the pegs, T its tension, and x = L the bridge. The bridge shakes the wooden body, which pushes the air. The force acts at each instant, so it keeps every frequency and weights the string’s n-th shape by its slope at the bridge, of size T\,n\pi/L for the shape \sin(n\pi x/L) of the next section.
2 N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 10 (bowed string instruments: the bridge).

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
The string’s shapes
The string’s frequencies are the frequencies of its own shapes. With mass \mu per unit length, Newton’s law gives the wave equation of post 2,3 
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -Au, \qquad Au = -c^2u_{xx}, \\
c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu},
\end{gathered}
 for shapes with u(0) = u(L) = 0. Each bit of string accelerates in proportion to how sharply it bends.
3 N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 2 (the vibrating string).The shapes that the operator A only stretches, its eigenfunctions, and their eigenvalues are 
\begin{gathered}
X_n(x) = \sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}, \qquad \lambda_n = \Big(\frac{n\pi c}{L}\Big)^2, \\
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = n f_1, \qquad f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} .
\end{gathered}
 Shape n has n arches and swings at exactly n times the lowest frequency. For a plucked string this is the only step that creates frequencies; bowed, this step decides which notes can sound, and the drive fixes the exact frequencies, at multiples of the playing frequency.



PreciselyThe shapes, step by step, and why there are no others derivatives, integration by parts

Solve AX = \lambda X, that is -c^2X'' = \lambda X with X(0) = X(L) = 0. Writing \lambda = c^2k^2 with k > 0, the solutions of X'' = -k^2X are a\cos kx + b\sin kx. The nut, X(0) = 0, forces a = 0; the bridge, X(L) = 0, then needs \sin kL = 0, so k = n\pi/L for n = 1, 2, 3, \dots This gives \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2 and f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = nc/2L.
No zero or negative \lambda occurs. Multiply -c^2X'' = \lambda X by X and integrate by parts; the boundary term vanishes because X = 0 at both ends, which leaves \lambda\int_0^L X^2\,dx = c^2\int_0^L (X')^2\,dx. A \lambda \le 0 would force X' = 0, so X would be a constant vanishing at the ends, that is X = 0. Each \lambda_n has multiplicity 1, since the nut removed the cosine. Post 2 shows that measured along these shapes the string falls apart into independent springs, and that every starting shape is a sum of them.


Released in any shape, the string moves as a sum of these shapes, each fading at its own rate 1/\tau_n: 
u = \sum_n a_n e^{-t/\tau_n} X_n(x)\cos(2\pi f_n t) .
 The start sets the amounts a_n. The fading rates are measured, not derived, and the high partials fade first.4
4 J. Wolfe, Strings, standing waves and harmonics, UNSW: high-frequency components “disappear quickly”, so a plucked note becomes “more mellow”.


DetailsWhere the equation comes from partial derivatives

Take the piece of string from x to x + dx, of mass \mu\,dx. The tension T pulls along the string at both ends; for a small slope, the sideways part of each pull is T times the slope u_x. The net sideways force is therefore T\,u_x(x + dx) - T\,u_x(x) \approx T\,u_{xx}\,dx, and Newton’s law sets it equal to mass times acceleration, \mu\,dx\,u_{tt}. Dividing by \mu\,dx gives u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} with c^2 = T/\mu. The nut and the bridge hold the ends still, u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0. The model assumes a perfectly flexible string, small slopes, no air and no friction; post 2 draws the forces.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
The chain in one line
Put together, partial n of a plucked string reaches your ear with the size 
c_n = |H(f_n)| \cdot \frac{Tn\pi}{L} \cdot |a_n| ,
 where H(f_n) is the filter’s factor. Pitch traces back to the spectrum of A; timbre to the start, the bridge’s weight, H and the spacing of the spectrum; loudness to the overall scale; duration to the losses, where the light touch acts.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
What the light touch does
A light touch keeps only the shapes that stand still under the finger. The finger is soft and lossy: it takes energy from whatever moves under it, but it does not hold the string still, as a new end would. A finger at x_f raises the fading rate of shape n in proportion to X_n(x_f)^2, how much that shape moves under it. A shape with a still point, a node, under the finger rings on; every other shape dies within a moment.
At the middle, X_n(L/2) = \sin(n\pi/2) is zero exactly when n is even. The survivors swing at 2f_1, 4f_1, 6f_1, \dots: the note an octave up. At a third, the survivors are n = 3, 6, 9, \dots, multiples of 3f_1: an octave and a fifth up.



PreciselyWhy the drain rate is X_n(x_f)^2 matrices

A friction force -r\,u_t(x_f, t) at the one point x_f turns post 2’s separate springs into q_n'' + \sum_m C_{nm}q_m' + \lambda_nq_n = 0 with C_{nm} \propto r\,X_n(x_f)X_m(x_f) (post 2). A shape with X_n(x_f) = 0 has a zero row and column in C, so it rings on untouched. For a light touch C is small, its off-diagonal entries matter only to second order, and each other shape drains at the rate C_{nn} \propto X_n(x_f)^2, the rule the piano page uses for felt dampers. The demo adds 45 per second times X_n(x_f)^2 to each shape’s own fading rate.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
section: Where you pluck sets the brightness
text:
Where you pluck sets the brightness
Plucking near the bridge sounds bright; plucking at the middle sounds hollow. A string pulled at the point x_0 into a triangle u_0 of height u_0(x_0) and let go at rest starts shape n with the amount 
a_n = \frac{2u_0(x_0)\,L^2}{\pi^2 x_0(L - x_0)}\cdot\frac{\sin(n\pi x_0/L)}{n^2},
 post 2’s pluck formula. Shape n pushes the bridge with a_n times the chain’s bridge weight, that is, in proportion to \sin(n\pi x_0/L)/n.
Near the bridge, x_0 \approx L and |\sin(n\pi x_0/L)| \approx n\pi(L - x_0)/L for the first several shapes, so they push the bridge about equally hard: a bright sound. At the middle, the even shapes stand still where you pulled and are missing, and the rest fall off like 1/n: a hollow sound.


  
  The open string, plucked 0.16 of its length from the bridge: mode n at n times the lowest frequency, exactly on line n, drawn as far as it swings just after the pluck.





DetailsWhere the pluck formula comes from integration by parts

The coefficient is a_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L u_0\,X_n\,dx, since the sines are perpendicular: \int_0^L X_mX_n\,dx = 0 for m \ne n. The plucked triangle u_0 is straight on each side of x_0, so integrating by parts twice on each piece leaves only the jump in slope at the corner, from u_0(x_0)/x_0 to -u_0(x_0)/(L - x_0), times X_n(x_0)(L/n\pi)^2. That is the formula above, and the 1/n^2 comes from the single corner. Measuring x_0 from the bridge instead, as the demo’s slider does, only flips the sign of every second a_n, because \sin(n\pi(L - x_0)/L) = \pm\sin(n\pi x_0/L); signs do not change how loud a shape is.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
section: Pressing down makes a new end
text:
Pressing down makes a new end
A finger pressed onto the fingerboard ties the string down there. Only the piece between finger and bridge sounds, and by the formula for f_1 the pitch rises in inverse proportion to its length: half the length sounds an octave up, two thirds a fifth up. Play a whole violin, bowed or plucked:


  
  
    Bow (hold)Pizzicato, plucked (tap)
     Wooden body
    Press and hold a string. Slide left and right to finger it.
  
  
  Left edge: the nut; right edge: the bridge. Ticks: where the finger goes for each semitone (fold below). Stems: the partials you hear; switching the body off or on changes their heights, never their positions.





DetailsWhere the finger goes for each semitone powers

An open string is one not pressed down by a finger. With the finger at distance d from the nut, the vibrating length shrinks to L - d, so the pitch rises by the factor L/(L - d). In equal temperament the twelve semitones of an octave are equal frequency ratios, each 2^{1/12}, so k semitones are 2^{k/12}. Solving L/(L - d) = 2^{k/12} gives d_k = (1 - 2^{-k/12})L: the positions bunch together toward the bridge. These are the ticks on the violin’s fingerboard above.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
The bow: one repeating cycle
A bowed string repeats one cycle exactly, so its partials sit exactly on the whole-number lines (post 1). The bow grips the string, drags it until it tears free, and grips it again, once per cycle. Hermann von Helmholtz saw the result in 1860:5 two straight pieces joined by one sharp corner, which races between bridge and finger and back, Helmholtz motion. The corner runs at the wave speed c, so the round trip of 2L takes 2L/c = 1/f_1 seconds. As a sum of the string’s shapes, 
u(x, t) \propto \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{1}{n^2}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\sin(2\pi n f_1 t) .

5 H. Helmholtz, “On the motion of the strings of a violin”, Proceedings of the Philosophical Society of Glasgow 5 (1860–64), 17–21, read 19 December 1860 (archive.org).

    
    BowedPlucked at 1/4
    
    Slowed about 500 times. The faint lens-shaped outline is the path the corner traces. Stems: the partials of the push on the bridge.
  




DetailsHelmholtz motion as a sum of modes the pluck formula above

A vibration microscope’s lens rides on a vibrating tuning fork, so that a bright speck on the string traces a pattern revealing its motion. Helmholtz reported what he saw in 1860 (H. Helmholtz, “On the motion of the strings of a violin”, Proceedings of the Philosophical Society of Glasgow 5 (1860–64), 17–21, read 19 December 1860, archive.org) and in his 1863 book (H. von Helmholtz, On the Sensations of Tone, translated by A. J. Ellis, 2nd English ed., Longmans, Green, 1895).
At each moment the string is two straight pieces, like a plucked string, with the corner at some point x_c. Helmholtz showed that the corner’s height is proportional to x_c(L - x_c), so it traces two arcs of a parabola, the lens in the demo, and that the corner moves at the wave speed c = 2Lf_1. Put that height in place of u_0(x_0) in the pluck formula with x_0 = x_c: the factor x_c(L - x_c) cancels, leaving a_n \propto \sin(n\pi x_c/L)/n^2. With x_c = 2Lf_1t this is \sin(2\pi nf_1t)/n^2. On the way back the corner runs along the lower arc, and the same formula covers it: for x_c between L and 2L, \sin(n\pi x_c/L) describes a corner at 2L - x_c with negative height. The force on the bridge is proportional to the slope there, and the slope of \sin(n\pi x/L) carries an extra factor n\pi/L, so partial n pushes the bridge in proportion to 1/n.


The locking comes from the bow’s friction, which is not linear: a self-sustained oscillation (appendix), not derived here. The player shapes the note: faster bowing, or bowing nearer the bridge, makes it louder, more force makes it brighter, and only a limited range of force keeps Helmholtz motion going at all.6
6 J. Wolfe, Bows and strings, UNSW: “if you bow with greater speed, the stick point will travel further and the amplitude will be greater”; the amplitude grows “as you move the bowing point towards the bridge”; “with more applied force, you excite more higher harmonics”; only a range of force sustains Helmholtz motion. See also Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 10 (bowed strings).


DetailsHow bow and string lock together

A real string is slightly stiff, so its own frequencies run a little sharp of the lines (the piano page); bowed, its motion is still “nearly exactly periodic”, so the bow pulls the partials onto the lines (J. Wolfe, Bows and strings, UNSW). The bow adds a friction force at one point, which depends on how fast the string slips past the hair there. How the two lock into Helmholtz motion is observed and reproduced in computer models (M. E. McIntyre, R. T. Schumacher and J. Woodhouse, “On the oscillations of musical instruments”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 74 (1983), 1325–1345; N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 10). The demo’s bowed voice adds a gentle vibrato, as players do, which wobbles the lines slightly (J. Wolfe, Articulation and vibrato on the violin, UNSW).

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?

title: A Piano
text:
This is an upright piano with its front panels and lid off: 88 keys, three pedals, 229 strings (as modelled here), and the action, the levers that link each key to its hammer and damper. It follows a Yamaha U1, 152 × 122 × 61 cm [1], with standard key widths [14, 15]. Strike a key and the graphs show its string moving and each mode’s strength; the sound is computed live from a stiff-string model. Made in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic’s AI model.
To play, hold a key in the 3D view or on the strip below and let go to damp it; on a computer, A to ’ play an octave, Z and X shift it, and Space holds the sustain pedal.

title: A Piano
text:
What you are seeing
The hammer starts the modes. A string fixed at both ends moves as a sum of modes, shapes sin(nπx/L) each swinging at its own frequency. The jack, a lever in each key’s action, throws the hammer and slips out from under it, so the hammer hits the string in free flight and falls back at once [19]. That push sets how strongly each mode rings; once the hammer has left the string, it cannot add a frequency the string does not already have (in this linear model). Books commonly give 1/7 to 1/9 of the way along, though on modern pianos many notes are struck nearer the end, at 1/12 to 1/17 [11]; the model uses 1/8, a node (a point that does not move) of modes 8 and 16, which stay silent.
The damper. Releasing a key returns a felt damper to its strings, just below the hammer [7]. To a good approximation, each mode then dies at a rate set by how much it moves under the felt (the orange ticks); the felt covers about 5 cm of string (less on short strings), so every mode is caught. Pianos leave about the top octave and a half undamped, as those short strings die quickly [12, 13]; this model leaves the top 20 keys, F6 to C8.
The three pedals. On an upright the left (soft) pedal moves the hammer rail toward the strings, so the hammers swing a shorter way and land more gently. The middle (practice mute) pedal drops a felt strip between hammers and strings. The right (sustain) pedal lifts every damper [1, 8, 9, 10]. None changes a string’s tension or stiffness, so none changes its frequencies.
The strings. On a typical piano, and in this model, the lowest 10 notes have one string, the next 15 two, the rest three [3]; the bass strings are copper-wound [2] and overstrung, crossing the tenor strings on a bridge of their own [6, 8, 10].
A stiff string. Thick steel wire also resists bending, which puts each partial (each frequency in the note) slightly sharp of a whole-number multiple, f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + B n^2} [5], where f₀ is the frequency the string would have without stiffness. B is least mid-keyboard and grows toward both ends [16, 17]. Tuners therefore stretch octaves slightly wider than 2 : 1 [18], which reduces the beating (a slow wobble in loudness) between the lower note’s sharp partials and the note above [17, 20].
Left out: each note is one ideal stiff string with pinned ends, with no coupling between strings and no soundboard resonances. The hammer is a brief push at one point (its felt’s nonlinearity is ignored); the damper felt is a uniform strip. B and the decay times are chosen by hand, not measured, and B here only rises toward the treble. String lengths other than the longest (119 cm) and a parlour grand’s shortest string (5.2 cm) [1, 4] are illustrative.
Read more: The Shape of a Sound, post 3: the piano, and why tuners stretch octaves.

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
text: Throughout this article, we use the following notations:

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
text:
1 Background

Proposition 1 For any random variable X, we have 
    X = F_X^{-1}(U).



Proof. For any x, we have 
    P(X \le x) = F_X(x) = P(U \le F_X(x)) = P(F_X^{-1}(U) \le x).
 Thus X = F_X^{-1}(U).

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
section: 2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
text:
2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
Now, we want to perform uniform sampling on the unit disk. We use polar coordinates; more specifically, we take r\cos(\theta), r\sin(\theta), where

r \in [0,1] such that P(r) \propto r (\Rightarrow P(r) = 2r)
\theta \sim U(0,2\pi)

The key lies in 1., that is, how to sample r such that P(r) = 2r. Let X be the random variable such that P(X = r) = 2r. Then, F_X(x) = \int_0^x 2r\,dr = x^2, and thus F_X^{-1}(y) = \sqrt{y}.

2.1 Code
With above in mind, we sample 10000 points on the unit disk, see Figure 1.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Sample the points
N = 10000
inv_cdf = lambda x: np.sqrt(x)
R = np.vectorize(inv_cdf)(np.random.uniform(0, 1, N))
T = np.random.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, N)
points = [(r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t)) for r, t in zip(R, T)]

# 2. Make a scatter plot
x, y = zip(*points)
plt.scatter(x, y, s=1)
plt.xticks([])
plt.yticks([])
ax = plt.gca()
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['bottom'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['left'].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
text: Using a few examples, we demonstrate how to conditionally break out of nested for loop using for-else clause.

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
How to Break Nested For Loop
text:
2 Double Nested for Loop
Here, the program halts right after (i,j) reaches (2,1), which is what we want.

for i in range(4): # Layer 1
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3): # Layer 2
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: finished")
        continue # continuing for the enclosing for loop (layer 1), thus ignoring the "break"
    break # reached <=> continue was not called <=> for loop layer 2 was broken

Here, no continue in the else part. Thus, the program breaks unconditionally after finishing its job in the i==0 round.

for i in range(4):
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3):
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> the for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: completed")
    break # always reached at i = 0

OK, we’ve learnt enough. Now, let’s test it on a triple nested for loop!

for i in range(3):

title: One string, end to end
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← 1 · What you hear · 3 · Other instruments, same recipe → · Glossary
A plucked string moves as a sum of simple shapes, one arch, two arches, three arches and so on, and the shape with n arches swings at exactly n times the lowest frequency.
This post follows the sound back from your ear, through the soundboard (a large thin wooden panel) and the bridge on it, to the string.

title: One string, end to end
text:
What you hear
You hear the air pressure p(t) at your ear, a sum of fading partials c_n e^{-t/\tau_n}\sin(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n) with frequencies f_n, amounts c_n, fading times \tau_n and phases \varphi_n. Pitch, loudness, timbre and duration are read off these numbers (post 1).

title: One string, end to end
text:
From force to sound
A string about 1 mm thick cannot move the air itself; the air simply flows around it.1 On a piano or guitar the bridge is a hardwood strip glued to the soundboard; on a violin it is a carved maple piece standing on the top plate, held there by the strings’ pressure.2 The bridge does move, just much less than the string: too little to change the string’s motion, which is why the string model below ties it down, but enough to drive the soundboard.
1 A. Askenfelt (ed.), Five Lectures on the Acoustics of the Piano, Royal Swedish Academy of Music, 1990, “Introduction”: “as the thin string cannot radiate a sound wave itself”.2 N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapters 9 (guitars), 10 (bowed string instruments) and 12 (the piano).The soundboard and the room turn the force F(t) with which the string pushes the bridge into the pressure at your ear, by a fixed linear filter: 
p(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} h(t - s)\,F(s)\,ds ,
 written p = h * F, a convolution. Here h is what a tap test records: on a silent instrument, tap the bridge once, sharply, and record the pressure at your ear, per unit of the tap’s strength (force times duration). During a note, the string’s push is a continuous run of such taps, each heard as a copy of h, delayed and scaled, and p is the sum of the copies. The filter is fixed and linear because small motions of the board and the air obey linear equations, nothing in them changes in time, and nothing can happen before its cause, which is why the integral stops at s = t.
Because the filter does not change in time, the pure tones e^{2\pi i f t} = \cos 2\pi f t + i\sin 2\pi f t (Euler’s formula) are its eigenfunctions. Substituting \tau = t - s, 
\begin{gathered}
\int_{-\infty}^{t} h(t - s)\,e^{2\pi i f s}\,ds = H(f)\,e^{2\pi i f t},\\
H(f) = \int_0^{\infty} h(\tau)\,e^{-2\pi i f \tau}\,d\tau ,
\end{gathered}
 so the eigenvalue is H(f), the Fourier transform of h. Taking real parts, each tone in F (next section: tones at the string’s f_n) keeps its frequency in p, multiplied by the size |H(f_n)| of this complex number and shifted in time, once the board’s brief ring at the start has died away (fold).3
3 A. V. Oppenheim and A. S. Willsky, with S. H. Nawab, Signals and Systems, 2nd ed., Prentice Hall, 1997, sections 2.2 (the convolution integral) and 3.2 (the response of linear time-invariant systems to complex exponentials).


PreciselyThe exact shift, and the start of the note complex numbers, integrals

Since h is real, the real parts say that \cos 2\pi f t comes out as |H(f)|\cos\big(2\pi f t + \arg H(f)\big), where \arg H(f) is the angle of H(f).
F is a sum of tones only from t = 0; before, it is the steady pull F(0) of the held string. A steady push makes no sound, H(0) = \int_0^\infty h = 0, so p(t) = \int_0^t h(t - s)\big(F(s) - F(0)\big)\,ds. This differs from the sum of rescaled tones only by integrals of h over lags longer than t, which vanish once the tap’s own ring has died away. Until then the board also rings at its own frequencies; after that, p is exactly the sum of rescaled tones.

title: One string, end to end
text:
From string to force
The force on the bridge depends only on the string’s slope there: 
F(t) = -T\,u_x(L, t),
 where u(x, t) is the string’s height at point x and time t, x = L is the bridge end, T is the tension and u_x the slope (set up below).
The string’s motion is u = \sum_n a_n\cos(2\pi f_n t)\,X_n(x), with shapes X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L) and amounts a_n set by the pluck (derived below), so 
F(t) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1}\,\frac{n\pi T}{L}\,a_n \cos 2\pi f_n t .
 The map from u to F acts at each instant, so it keeps every frequency and only weights shape n, by -T X_n'(L) = \pm Tn\pi/L. So you pluck once, but the string pushes the bridge up and down hundreds of times a second, for seconds (262 times a second for middle C); for a sharp pluck, F is a rectangular wave (the figure’s middle row).

A string tuned to middle C (f₁ = 262 Hz), plucked a fifth of the way from the nut, over its first 30 ms. Top: the finger lets go once, at t = 0. Middle: the force on the bridge, computed from the pluck series; it first changes when the pluck's corner, travelling along the string at the wave speed c derived below, reaches the bridge after about 1.5 ms, then keeps oscillating. Bottom: the pressure at an ear 1 m away: the same frequencies in a different mix, about 3 ms later. Before t = 0 the finger holds the bent string still, so the forces are steady. The rows are scaled separately, and the bottom row's mix is illustrative.



PreciselyWhy F = -T u_x(L, t), and why the bridge carries every shape integrals

The string touches the bridge only at x = L, and there the two pull on each other along the string’s direction with tension T. By the rule derived below, the upward part of the bridge’s pull on the string is T u_x(L, t), so by Newton’s third law the string pulls the bridge with F(t) = -T u_x(L, t). A check on the sign: a string bulging up near the bridge has u_x(L, t) < 0, so F > 0, and it pulls the bridge up.
A check that nothing else acts: multiply the string’s equation (below) by its mass per unit length \mu, giving \mu u_{tt} = T u_{xx}, and integrate over the string. The string’s total upward momentum, P(t) = \int_0^L \mu\,u_t\,dx, then changes at the rate 
P'(t) = T u_x(L, t) - T u_x(0, t) ,
 which is exactly the bridge’s pull plus the nut’s, -T u_x(0, t) by the same rule.
One point of the string, u(x_1, t), misses every shape with a still point at x_1: at the middle, every even shape. The bridge misses none, because the slope X_n'(L) = (-1)^n n\pi/L is never zero. So F contains every shape the pluck started.

title: One string, end to end
text:
The string
For a plucked string, this is the only step that creates the frequencies. The reason: measured along the shapes X_n, the string’s equation falls apart into separate springs, one per shape, and these are the only shapes that do this.

The problem
Pull a string aside at one point and let go: we want its height u(x, t) for all x and all t \ge 0. The string runs from the nut at x = 0, fixed to the heavy neck (on a piano, a bar on the iron frame), to the bridge at x = L, and the model ties both ends down. Four facts pin u down: 
\begin{aligned}
&u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx} &&\text{Newton's law},\\
&u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0 &&\text{tied ends},\\
&u(x, 0) = u_0(x) &&\text{plucked shape},\\
&u_t(x, 0) = 0 &&\text{let go at rest}.
\end{aligned}
 Subscripts are partial derivatives: u_{tt} is the acceleration of the point at x, and u_{xx} is how sharply the string curves there. So the first line says that each bit of string accelerates in proportion to its curvature, with a constant c^2 found in the next section. The tied ends are a boundary condition: they hold at the edges for all time, while the start holds everywhere at one moment.


Where the equation comes from
Newton’s law on a short piece of string gives the first line.4
4 N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 2 (the vibrating string).
  
  
  
  
  
  TT
  xx + dx
  upward part of each pull ≈ T × slope

The string has tension T and mass \mu per unit length. The piece from x to x + dx is pulled along the string at each end with force T, and for a small slope the upward part of that pull is T times the slope u_x. So the net upward force is T u_x(x + dx) - T u_x(x) \approx T u_{xx}\,dx, and it equals mass times acceleration, \mu\,dx\,u_{tt}: 
u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}, \qquad c = \sqrt{T/\mu} .
 The model assumes a perfectly flexible string, small slopes and no friction (friction comes back below).


The whole idea with two beads
With two beads in place of the string, the whole idea fits in a 2 \times 2 matrix.
Put two beads on a weightless string, at a third and two thirds of the way along, each carrying a third of the string’s mass, m = \mu L/3. Call their heights u_1 and u_2. Each bead is pulled toward its neighbours, the tied ends counting as neighbours at height zero, so with spacing \ell = L/3, 
\begin{gathered}
\begin{pmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{pmatrix}'' = -K \begin{pmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{pmatrix},\\
K = \frac{T}{m\ell}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} .
\end{gathered}
 Each bead’s acceleration depends on the other’s height: the motion is coupled.
Now measure along two other directions: both beads together, q_1 = (u_1 + u_2)/\sqrt2, and the beads opposite, q_2 = (u_1 - u_2)/\sqrt2. Adding and subtracting the two equations gives 
q_1'' = -\frac{T}{m\ell}\,q_1, \qquad q_2'' = -\frac{3T}{m\ell}\,q_2 .
 Two separate springs, with frequencies in the ratio 1 : \sqrt3; every motion of the beads is the two swings added.


  
    
    
  
  
    Together: q₁ only
    Opposite: q₂ only
    A mix
    Hear this motion
  
  Slowed down. Right: the plane of the two heights, u₁ across and u₂ up. A mix traces a tangle; started along q₁ or q₂ alone, the motion runs straight along that tilted line. The sound puts the q₁ swing at 196 Hz.


These directions work because K only stretches them: K(1, 1) = \frac{T}{m\ell}(1, 1) and K(1, -1) = \frac{3T}{m\ell}(1, -1). They are the eigenvectors of K, and the stretch factors, its eigenvalues, are the springs’ stiffnesses. They are also the string’s first two shapes, one arch and two arches, sampled at the beads; the string is the same calculation with infinitely many beads.



PreciselyMore beads, and the limit matrices and limits

With N beads, spacing \ell = L/(N+1) and m = \mu\ell, the matrix is K = \frac{T}{m\ell}\,\mathrm{tridiag}(-1, 2, -1). Its eigenvectors are the sines \sin(n\pi x/L) sampled at the beads, with eigenvalues \frac{c^2}{\ell^2}\,4\sin^2\frac{n\pi\ell}{2L}, which tend to the string’s (n\pi c/L)^2 as N \to \infty. (The frequency ratios tend to 1 : 2 : 3 whatever the beads weigh; the frequencies themselves need m = \mu\ell.) Each row of the bead equation tends to u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}, by Taylor’s theorem.




The string: the same move
For the string, the column of two heights becomes the whole curve u(\cdot, t), and the matrix K becomes the operator 
\begin{gathered}
A u = -c^2\,u_{xx},\\
\text{for shapes with } u(0) = u(L) = 0 ,
\end{gathered}
 so the equation reads u_{tt} = -Au, and the tied ends are part of A.
The shapes that A only stretches. Solve AX = \lambda X, that is X'' = -k^2X with k^2 = \lambda/c^2 and X(0) = X(L) = 0. The solutions are C_1\cos kx + C_2\sin kx; the end x = 0 kills the cosine, and the end x = L needs \sin kL = 0, so kL = n\pi. (No \lambda \le 0 works; the first fold below shows why.) So the eigenfunctions of A and their eigenvalues are 
\begin{gathered}
X_n(x) = \sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}, \qquad \lambda_n = \Big(\frac{n\pi c}{L}\Big)^2,\\
n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
\end{gathered}
 Shape n has n arches.
Coordinates along them. Measure the string by how much of each shape it contains, q_n(t) = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L u(x, t)\,X_n(x)\,dx, the continuous version of q_1 = (u_1 + u_2)/\sqrt2. Then each coordinate is a spring: 
\begin{aligned}
q_n'' &= \tfrac{2}{L}\!\int_0^L u_{tt}X_n = \tfrac{2}{L}\!\int_0^L c^2u_{xx}X_n\\
&= \tfrac{2}{L}\!\int_0^L c^2u\,X_n'' = -\lambda_n\,q_n .
\end{aligned}
 The middle step integrates by parts twice, moving both derivatives onto X_n; the boundary terms vanish because u and X_n are zero at the ends. (A pluck’s corner has no u_{xx}; the second fold below handles it.) The last step is X_n'' = -(\lambda_n/c^2)X_n. So spring n swings at 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{n c}{2L} = n f_1 .

Why only these shapes. Take any other family of perpendicular shapes \psi_1, \psi_2, \dots that vanish at the ends and build every shape (an orthonormal basis), with coordinates q_i = \int u\,\psi_i. The same calculation gives q_i'' = -\sum_j M_{ij}\,q_j with M_{ij} = \int (A\psi_j)\psi_i: each coordinate feels the others, as u_1 and u_2 did. The coordinates come apart exactly when M is diagonal, which happens exactly when every \psi_j is an eigenfunction. Nothing about the form of the solution was assumed.
Why these shapes are enough. Every starting shape is a sum of sines, u_0 = \sum a_n X_n: the Fourier sine series, the one theorem this post quotes rather than proves.5
5 E. M. Stein and R. Shakarchi, Fourier Analysis: An Introduction, Princeton University Press, 2003, chapters 2–3 (Fejér’s theorem; mean-square convergence). A shape on [0, L] extended to an odd function of period 2L has a Fourier series of sines only.


PreciselyDecoupling happens exactly in an eigenbasis inner products, orthonormal bases

Write \langle u, w\rangle = \int_0^L u\,w\,dx. (The main text’s sines are orthogonal but have \int X_n^2 = L/2; normalised, \sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(n\pi x/L), the factor 2/L in q_n disappears.) For shapes u, w vanishing at the ends, two integrations by parts give \langle Au, w\rangle = c^2\!\int u'w' = \langle u, Aw\rangle: A is symmetric, like K. With w = u, \langle Au, u\rangle = c^2\!\int (u')^2 > 0 unless u' is identically zero, which with u(0) = 0 forces u = 0; so A is positive, and AX = \lambda X forces \lambda > 0. That is why no \lambda \le 0 appears above.
Proposition. Let \psi_1, \psi_2, \dots be an orthonormal basis of square-integrable shapes, each twice differentiable and zero at the ends, and let q_j = \langle u, \psi_j\rangle. Then q_i'' = -\sum_j M_{ij}q_j with M_{ij} = \langle A\psi_j, \psi_i\rangle, and M is diagonal if and only if every \psi_j is an eigenfunction of A.
Proof. For a smooth solution, q_i'' = \langle u_{tt}, \psi_i\rangle = -\langle Au, \psi_i\rangle = -\langle u, A\psi_i\rangle, by symmetry of A; for a pluck, q_i'' = -\langle u, A\psi_i\rangle is the definition of solution in the next fold, with \varphi = \psi_i. Expanding u = \sum_j q_j\psi_j gives q_i'' = -\sum_j q_j\langle\psi_j, A\psi_i\rangle = -\sum_j M_{ij}q_j. If A\psi_j = \kappa_j\psi_j for every j, then M_{ij} = \kappa_j\langle\psi_j, \psi_i\rangle is diagonal. Conversely, A\psi_j = \sum_i M_{ij}\psi_i (expansion in the basis), which is M_{jj}\psi_j when M is diagonal. \square
In a basis of polynomials vanishing at the ends (Gram–Schmidt on x(L - x)x^k), M has nonzero entries far from the diagonal; with L = 1 its top-left entry is 10c^2, just above \lambda_1 = \pi^2c^2 \approx 9.87c^2.





PreciselyWhat “solution” means for a pluck, and why there is exactly one integration by parts, Cauchy–Schwarz

The triangle has a corner, where u_{xx} does not exist, so the equation cannot hold there literally. The calculation of q_n'' above never needed u_{xx} once the derivatives were moved onto X_n, which suggests the definition. A solution is a shape u(t) with \int u^2 < \infty, changing continuously in mean square, such that for every smooth \varphi vanishing at the ends, \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\langle u, \varphi\rangle = -\langle u, A\varphi\rangle, with \langle u(0), \varphi\rangle = \langle u_0, \varphi\rangle and \frac{d}{dt}\langle u, \varphi\rangle(0) = \langle v_0, \varphi\rangle, where v_0 is the starting velocity (zero for a pluck). Smooth solutions satisfy it (integrate by parts); testing against all such \varphi loses nothing, because they are dense in mean square. (L. C. Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed., AMS, 2010, section 7.2)
Uniqueness. With \varphi = X_n, each q_n solves q_n'' = -\lambda_nq_n with given q_n(0), q_n'(0). That has exactly one solution: the difference r of two has r(0) = r'(0) = 0, and E = (r')^2 + \lambda_nr^2 has E' = 0, so r = 0. Two solutions with the same start therefore have the same coordinates, so they are equal (the sines are a basis).
Existence. The series \sum_n (a_n\cos\omega_nt + b_n\sin\omega_nt)X_n, with \omega_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}, a_n = \frac{2}{L}\int u_0X_n and b_n = \frac{2}{L}\int v_0X_n/\omega_n, is a solution when the start has finite energy, \int(u_0')^2 < \infty and \int v_0^2 < \infty. Integration by parts and Bessel’s inequality give \sum n^2a_n^2 < \infty, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives \sum |a_n| + |b_n| < \infty; the series and its term-by-term time derivatives against \varphi then converge uniformly, and the defining identity holds.
Counting. A mass on a spring has one eigenvalue and a two-dimensional space of motions (\cos and \sin); two beads have two eigenvalues and four; the string has two dimensions of motion for each eigenvalue.




The pluck
Each spring starts where the pluck puts it, at rest, so q_n(t) = a_n\cos(2\pi f_n t) and 
\begin{gathered}
u(x, t) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} a_n \cos(2\pi f_n t)\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L},\\
a_n = \frac{2u_0(x_0)\,L^2\,\sin(n\pi x_0/L)}{\pi^2 n^2\,x_0(L - x_0)} ,
\end{gathered}
 for a triangle with its apex above x_0, at height u_0(x_0). This is the motion in the demo at the top.
a_n = 0 when nx_0/L is a whole number: a shape with a still point exactly where you pluck is never started. Pluck a fifth of the way along and the 5th, 10th, 15th, … shapes are missing.



DetailsThe coefficients, and the exact motion integration by parts

a_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L u_0 X_n. The triangle is straight on both sides of x_0, where its slope jumps by -u_0(x_0)L/(x_0(L - x_0)); integrating by parts twice turns the integral into that jump times X_n(x_0)\,(L/n\pi)^2, which is the formula above.
The dashed curve in the demo is the exact motion in d’Alembert’s form: extend u_0 to an odd function \tilde u_0 of period 2L; then u(x, t) = \frac12\big(\tilde u_0(x - ct) + \tilde u_0(x + ct)\big), two copies of the triangle running in opposite directions and flipping over at the ends. (J. le Rond d’Alembert, “Recherches sur la courbe que forme une corde tenduë mise en vibration”, Histoire de l’Académie royale des sciences et belles-lettres de Berlin 3, 1747, published 1749, 214–219) Its sine series is the series above, since \frac12[\sin(\theta - \phi) + \sin(\theta + \phi)] = \sin\theta\cos\phi. The corners travel, which is why a solution has to be defined without u_{xx}.

title: One string, end to end
text:
The chain in one line
In one line, the amount of partial n at your ear is 
c_n = |H(f_n)| \cdot \frac{Tn\pi}{L} \cdot |a_n| ,
 the soundboard’s factor times the bridge’s weight times what the pluck gave shape n. The four aspects trace back:

pitch to the spectrum of A: f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = nf_1;
timbre to the three factors and the spacing of the spectrum;
loudness to how far you pull the string, u_0(x_0);
duration to the losses (next section).

Three everyday facts follow: two from n|a_n| \propto |\sin(n\pi x_0/L)|/n, since |H(f_n)| is fixed for a given instrument, and one from f_1.

Pluck near an end and it sounds bright. For small x_0, \sin(n\pi x_0/L)/n \approx \pi x_0/L for many n: many high partials, all about equally strong. Pluck at the middle and the even partials vanish: a hollow sound.
A fingertip sounds mellower than a pick. A fingertip leaves a rounded start with no corner, so the a_n fall off faster than 1/n^2 and the high partials are weaker.
Shorter, tighter or lighter strings sound higher. f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}: Mersenne’s laws of 1636.6

6 M. Mersenne, Harmonie universelle, S. Cramoisy, Paris, 1636–1637.

  
  Pluck point x₀0.20 L
  
    Touch lightly at
    no touch1/21/31/41/5
